facts.t: Brettus adonis and B. cingulatus invade other spiders' webs, vibrate the silk to deceive the owner, then eat it, its prey or its eggs.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Hallas SEA (1986) Predatory versatility and intraspecific interactions of spartaeine jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae): Brettus adonis, B. cingulatus, Cyrba algerina, and Phaeacius sp. indet. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 13: 491-520
facts.kp: invaded alien webs, acted as aggressive mimics by performing a variety of vibratory behaviours
facts.note: Abstract also lists kleptoparasitism (insects in webs) and oophagy. Same behaviour reported for Cyrba algerina (Australian-checklist genus Cyrba).

facts.t: Two Brettus species solved a novel escape test by trial and error, repeating a tactic that worked and switching after one that failed.
facts.cite: Cross FR, Jackson RR (2015) Solving a novel confinement problem by spartaeine salticids that are predisposed to solve problems in the context of predation. Animal Cognition 18: 509-515
facts.kp: proficient at solving the confinement problem by repeating 'correct' choices and by switching
facts.note: Shared result with Cyrba and Portia (aggressive mimics); Cocalus gibbosus and Paracyrba wanlessi did not solve it. Spider started on an island in water and could leap or swim.

facts.t: Even before maturity, male Carrhotus xanthogramma are heavier, more active and bolder than females of the same stage.
facts.cite: Mezőfi L, Markó V, Taranyi DÁ, Markó G (2023) Sex-specific life-history strategies among immature jumping spiders: differences in body parameters and behavior. Current Zoology 69: 535-551
facts.kp: Males were more active and more risk tolerant than females
facts.note: Immatures of a protandrous species; males also had larger prosoma.

facts.t: In trials, Colonus puerperus never ate the ant-mimicking Peckhamia picata and seemed to class it as an ant early in the hunt.
facts.cite: Durkee CA, Weiss MR, Uma DB (2011) Ant mimicry lessens predation on a North American jumping spider by larger salticid spiders. Environmental Entomology 40: 1223-1231
facts.kp: our focal predator did not consume any ant-mimicking spiders
facts.note: Paper calls it Thiodina puerpera; restored to Colonus puerperus (Hentz, 1846) by Bustamante, Maddison & Ruiz 2015 Zootaxa 4012 (doi 10.11646/zootaxa.4012.1.10).

facts.t: Corythalia conferta has been found living in a potter wasp's mud pot and in a chamber of an organ-pipe wasp's clay nest.
facts.cite: Giannotti E (2022) Notes on the nesting and prey capture habits of Corythalia conferta (Araneae: Salticidae) in urban area. Brazilian Journal of Science 1(10): 37-41
facts.kp: One spider was observed living inside a pot built by the wasp Zeta argillacea
facts.note: Second nest was of a Trypoxylon sp. ('organ tube'). Brazil. Small journal; two observations only. Abstract also notes a tendency to eat ants.

facts.t: On ginger leaves in New Guinea, Diolenius holds its very long first legs like fly wings and walks backwards like a fly.
facts.cite: Żabka M (1992) Orsima Simon (Araneae: Salticidae), a remarkable spider from Africa and Malaya. Bulletin of the British Arachnological Society 9(1): 10-12
facts.kp: the extremely long first legs are held in a way that imitates fly's wings
facts.note: Żabka's own field observation of 'Diolenius and related taxa' in Papua New Guinea, reported in a taxonomic paper on Orsima; anecdotal.

facts.t: Eris jumping spiders drink extrafloral nectar from partridge pea, and plants with resident jumping spiders set more seed.
facts.cite: Ruhren S, Handel SN (1999) Jumping spiders (Salticidae) enhance the seed production of a plant with extrafloral nectaries. Oecologia 119: 227-230
facts.kp: jumping spiders (Eris sp. and Metaphidippus sp.) on C. nictitans collected nectar
facts.note: Plant Chamaecrista nictitans (partridge pea; common name is mine). Seed effect is for jumping spiders generally (Eris sp. and Metaphidippus sp.), New Jersey, USA. Spiders spent 86% of time on plants with active nectaries.

facts.t: A sublethal insecticide dose made Eris militaris personalities about 23% less consistent without changing average behaviour.
facts.cite: Royauté R, Buddle CM, Vincent C (2015) Under the influence: sublethal exposure to an insecticide affects personality expression in a jumping spider. Functional Ecology 29: 962-970
facts.kp: insecticide-exposed individuals showed an average of 23% lower repeatability
facts.note: Organophosphate phosmet. Three authors per Crossref (Europe PMC adds the handling editor).

facts.t: Euophrys omnisuperstes, 'standing above all', was described from the upper slopes of Everest and Makalu, its holotype from about 5,900 m.
facts.cite: Wanless FR (1975) Spiders of the family Salticidae from the upper slopes of Everest and Makalu. Bulletin of the British Arachnological Society 3(5): 132-136
facts.kp: the specific name omnisuperstes (standing above all) ... Holotype male: Nepal/Tibet ... 19,500 ft
facts.note: 19,500 ft = 5,944 m. Name suggested by W.S. Bristowe. Country: Nepal/China (Tibet) border.

facts.t: Small salticids found at 6,700 m on Everest in 1924 seem to be Euophrys omnisuperstes, though too damaged to confirm.
facts.cite: Wanless FR (1975) Spiders of the family Salticidae from the upper slopes of Everest and Makalu. Bulletin of the British Arachnological Society 3(5): 132-136
facts.kp: immature specimens collected by Major Kingston from 22,000 ft ... appear to be conspecific
facts.note: 22,000 ft = 6,706 m; the source of the often-quoted '6,700 m' record. Wanless notes they are 'mutilated and badly rubbed'.

facts.t: Everest's high-altitude salticids feed on flies and springtails living on wind-blown plant debris, the end of a short food chain.
facts.cite: Wanless FR (1975) Spiders of the family Salticidae from the upper slopes of Everest and Makalu. Bulletin of the British Arachnological Society 3(5): 132-136
facts.kp: spiders being the only predators formed the last link in this simple food chain
facts.note: Wanless reports Swan's (1961) finding for the Himalayan salticid community generally, not E. omnisuperstes specifically; fact is worded for the Everest salticids. Card could say 'Euophrys on Everest...'.

facts.t: Habronattus pyrrithrix sees red via a retinal filter that shifts some green receptors to red, a mechanism unknown before in spiders.
facts.cite: Zurek DB, Cronin TW, Taylor LA, Byrne K, Sullivan MLG, Morehouse NI (2015) Spectral filtering enables trichromatic vision in colorful jumping spiders. Current Biology 25: R403-R404
facts.kp: a subset of their photoreceptors from green to red via a long-pass filter
facts.checked: read authors' PDF (Morehouse lab homepage, homepages.uc.edu)
facts.note: Correspondence, no abstract. Text says 'a mechanism previously unknown in spiders'. Gives trichromacy (UV, green, red).

facts.t: Courting Habronattus dossenus males pair each visual display with substrate vibrations: thumps, scrapes and buzzes.
facts.cite: Elias DO, Mason AC, Maddison WP, Hoy RR (2003) Seismic signals in a courting male jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Experimental Biology 206: 4029-4039
facts.kp: each prominent visual signal is accompanied by a subsequent seismic component ('thumps', 'scrapes' and 'buzzes')
facts.note: Seismic signals are produced by at least three independent mechanisms, separately from the visual signals.

facts.t: Habronattus dossenus males mated more often courting on leaf litter, which carries their vibrations, than on rock or desert sand.
facts.cite: Elias DO, Mason AC, Hoy RR (2004) The effect of substrate on the efficacy of seismic courtship signal transmission in the jumping spider Habronattus dossenus (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Experimental Biology 207: 4105-4110
facts.kp: males mating successfully was significantly higher on leaf litter than on rocks or desert sand

facts.t: Habronattus pugillis males differ in face colour, setae and dance from one Arizona sky-island range to the next, driven by sexual selection.
facts.cite: Masta SE, Maddison WP (2002) Sexual selection driving diversification in jumping spiders. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 99: 4442-4447
facts.where: abstract (PNAS) and abstract of Maddison & McMahon 2000 Syst Biol 49: 400-421
facts.kp: divergence in traits of male behavior and morphology ... attributed to sexual selection
facts.note: 'Arizona sky-island' detail comes from the companion paper (Maddison & McMahon 2000, doi 10.1080/10635159950127312): populations on nearby mountain ranges in southern Arizona differ in face colour, setae, carapace, courtship.

facts.t: Sex chromosome-autosome fusions arose at least 8 times within Habronattus, a remarkable number for such a small clade.
facts.cite: Maddison WP, Leduc-Robert G (2013) Multiple origins of sex chromosome fusions correlated with chiasma localization in Habronattus jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Evolution 67: 2258-2272
facts.kp: at least 8-15 gains ... of neo-Y ... a remarkable number
facts.note: Authors link this to sexual conflict and the complexity of male courtship. Taxonomic/cytogenetic; probably low appeal for the card.

facts.t: Heliophanus termitophagus eats termites in the wild but accepts a broader range of prey in the lab, making it a 'euryphagous specialist'.
facts.cite: Michálek O, Pekár S, Haddad CR (2021) Fundamental trophic niche of two prey-specialized jumping spiders, Cyrba algerina and Heliophanus termitophagus (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 49: 268-271
facts.kp: Both species accepted a broader spectrum of prey under laboratory conditions than in the field
facts.note: Field diet (realised niche) of termites from earlier data cited in the abstract. DOI from Crossref.

facts.t: Heliophanus cupreus and H. flavipes fed a lipid-rich diet survived better and then preferred aphids over spider prey.
facts.cite: Řezáč M, Gloríková N, Líznarová E, Wilder SM, Heneberg P (2026) The nutritional status of Heliophanus spiders shifts their food preferences for aphid prey over intraguild spider prey. Environmental Entomology 55: nvaf135
facts.kp: The lipid-rich diet increased spider survival and led to a preference for agricultural pest prey
facts.note: Spider prey was Dictyna; aphid Metopolophium dirhodum.

facts.t: Hyllus diardi, H. semicupreus and H. treleaveni have all been recorded preying on vertebrates, rare among jumping spiders.
facts.cite: Nyffeler M, Zamani A, Cutler B, Krysko KL (2025) Jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) attacking and eating vertebrates: an update. Journal of Arachnology 53: 143-149
facts.kp: attributed to seven species: Hyllus diardi ..., H. semicupreus ..., H. treleaveni
facts.note: Nyffeler et al. 2021 (doi 10.1636/joa-s-20-090): most cases are frogs and lizards. Prey of each Hyllus species not checked.

facts.t: Hyllus treleaveni is the largest jumping spider in Africa.
facts.cite: Wesołowska W, Cumming MS (2004) A redescription and natural history of Hyllus treleaveni Peckham et Peckham, 1902, the largest jumping spider in Africa (Araneae: Salticidae). Annales Zoologici 54: 579-586
facts.kp: the largest jumping spider in Africa
facts.checked: read title and abstract (Crossref metadata); body size not checked
facts.note: Abstract gives no size; full text would have measurements.

facts.t: In Lyssomanes viridis contests, the male with longer chelicerae usually wins; male chelicerae grow with strong positive allometry.
facts.cite: Tedore C, Johnsen S (2012) Weaponry, color, and contest success in the jumping spider Lyssomanes viridis. Behavioural Processes 89: 203-211
facts.kp: Males having longer chelicerae than their opponents were significantly more likely to win
facts.note: Smaller winners had less red chelicerae than their opponents.

facts.t: Lyssomanes viridis finds its leafy perch by light level and leaf brightness, not by the star shape or green of its sweetgum host.
facts.cite: Tedore C, Johnsen S (2016) Disentangling the visual cues used by a jumping spider to locate its microhabitat. Journal of Experimental Biology 219: 2396-2401
facts.kp: use ambient illumination and possibly perceived leaf brightness but not leaf shape or color
facts.note: Summer host Liquidambar styraciflua (sweetgum).

facts.t: Female pheromones speed up male Lyssomanes viridis in recognising images of their own species.
facts.cite: Tedore C, Johnsen S (2013) Pheromones exert top-down effects on visual recognition in the jumping spider Lyssomanes viridis. Journal of Experimental Biology 216: 1744-1756
facts.kp: Pheromones hastened the recognition of images with coloration and morphology closely matching those of conspecifics
facts.note: Males' template for a conspecific female was coarse; for a male face it was more specific.

facts.t: Maevia inclemens has two male forms: a tufted male that stilts and waves about 9 cm from a female, and a grey male that sidles at 3 cm.
facts.cite: Clark DL, Morjan CL (2001) Attracting female attention: the evolution of dimorphic courtship displays in the jumping spider Maevia inclemens (Araneae: Salticidae). Proceedings of the Royal Society B 268: 2461-2465
facts.kp: The tufted morph stilts and waves from an average distance of 9 cm
facts.note: Grey morph 'crouches and sidles from an average distance of 3 cm'. Each morph won female attention faster at its own distance.

facts.t: Maevia inclemens females carry two separate recognition templates, one for each male form, though both forms look the same size to her.
facts.cite: Clark DL, Uetz GW (1993) Signal efficacy and the evolution of male dimorphism in the jumping spider, Maevia inclemens. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 90: 11954-11957
facts.kp: females were determined to have two distinct male-recognition templates
facts.note: Abstract: the two displays present 'images that are almost identical in height and visual target area'. Tested with computer animation. PNAS archive is free.

facts.t: Courting grey males of Maevia inclemens are spotted by Phidippus audax from farther away than tufted males.
facts.cite: Clark DL, Simmons LA, Bowker RG (2018) Aspects of courtship risks and mating success in the dimorphic jumping spider, Maevia inclemens (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 46: 1-6
facts.kp: P. audax oriented to G at significantly greater distances than to T
facts.note: Tested with animations; grey males also courted less and later when a predator was near. DOI from Crossref.

facts.t: Maevia eureka, described from early-mid Miocene amber in Mexico, is the first known fossil of the genus.
facts.cite: Riquelme F, Menéndez-Acuña M (2017) Miocene spider Maevia eureka nov. sp. (Araneae: Salticidae). PeerJ 5: e3614
facts.kp: This represents the first known fossil species within Maevia
facts.note: Amber from Chiapas; closest to living Maevia poultoni.

facts.t: In Marpissa muscosa the tiny posterior median eyes feed straight to the arcuate body, suggesting they do not detect movement.
facts.cite: Steinhoff POM, Uhl G, Harzsch S, Sombke A (2020) Visual pathways in the brain of the jumping spider Marpissa muscosa. Journal of Comparative Neurology 528: 1883-1902
facts.kp: project directly to the arcuate body, suggesting ... posterior median eyes do not detect movement
facts.note: Unlike the other secondary eyes, which link to the mushroom body. Open access status assumed from bioRxiv preprint 10.1101/640706; check.

facts.t: On a treadmill, Marpissa muscosa needed its tracheae only at top running speed, when they boosted aerobic metabolism.
facts.cite: Schmitz A (2005) Spiders on a treadmill: influence of running activity on metabolic rates in Pardosa lugubris (Araneae, Lycosidae) and Marpissa muscosa (Araneae, Salticidae). Journal of Experimental Biology 208: 1401-1411
facts.kp: tracheae in M. muscosa support the aerobic metabolism only at the most intense physical exercise

facts.t: Naphrys pulex attacks ants head-on and prefers them even as motionless dead lures, without any prior experience of ants.
facts.cite: Li D, Jackson RR, Cutler B (1996) Prey-capture techniques and prey preferences of Habrocestum pulex, an ant-eating jumping spider (Araneae, Salticidae) from North America. Journal of Zoology 240: 551-562
facts.kp: Ants, but not other insects, were consistently attacked head-on
facts.note: Paper calls it Habrocestum pulex; WSC current name Naphrys pulex (Hentz, 1846), transferred from Habrocestum by Edwards 2003 (WSC search snippet). After attacking an ant it holds its forelegs extended off the ground.

facts.t: Orsima ichneumon is a reverse mimic: its abdomen tip and long, mobile spinnerets look like an insect's head with antennae.
facts.cite: Żabka M (1992) Orsima Simon (Araneae: Salticidae), a remarkable spider from Africa and Malaya. Bulletin of the British Arachnological Society 9(1): 10-12
facts.where: p. 10 (remarks on biology) and p. 11 (genus description)
facts.kp: The tip of the abdomen and spinnerets resemble an insect's head with appendages
facts.note: Żabka cites Reiskind (1976) and Preston-Mafham & Preston-Mafham (1984), who say it mimics mutillid wasps in reverse; genus description: spinnerets 'very movable, mimic insect's antennae'. Formerly known as Orsima formica.

facts.t: Orsima is known from both West-Central Africa and Malaya, a split range Żabka thought reflects an ancient range broken up.
facts.cite: Żabka M (1992) Orsima Simon (Araneae: Salticidae), a remarkable spider from Africa and Malaya. Bulletin of the British Arachnological Society 9(1): 10-12
facts.kp: Perhaps its present distribution reflects an ancient continuous range disrupted by climatic changes
facts.note: O. constricta from Congo, Gabon, Ivory Coast; O. ichneumon from Malaya. Author's hypothesis, worded as such. Species count may have changed since 1992.

facts.t: Paracyrba wanlessi lives inside hollow internodes of fallen bamboo and hunts mosquito larvae, pupae and adults.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Li D, Woon JR, Hashim R, Cross FR (2014) Intricate predatory decisions by a mosquito-specialist spider from Malaysia. Royal Society Open Science 1: 140131
facts.kp: lives in the hollow internodes of fallen bamboo and preys on ... mosquitoes

facts.t: Paracyrba wanlessi chooses mosquitoes over other prey in or out of water, even when raised on a diet without mosquitoes.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Li D, Woon JR, Hashim R, Cross FR (2014) Intricate predatory decisions by a mosquito-specialist spider from Malaysia. Royal Society Open Science 1: 140131
facts.kp: preference ... is expressed regardless of ... whether the diet includes or excludes mosquitoes
facts.note: Unlike Evarcha culicivora it showed no choice by mosquito species, sex or blood meal.

facts.t: Paraphidippus cf. aurantius has been seen attacking a bird hatchling that weighed about 4-6 times as much as the spider.
facts.cite: Nyffeler M, Edwards GB, Arkin R (2021) Vertebrate-eating jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) revisited: consumption of geckos and bird hatchlings. Journal of Arachnology 49: 397-401
facts.kp: attacking bird hatchlings ... weighing ≈4–6 times more than the spiders
facts.note: Abstract groups Paraphidippus cf. aurantius with Phidippus audax for the hatchling attacks (Paridae, Trochilidae); per-species detail not checked. Identification only 'cf.'.

facts.t: Peckhamia picata is also spared by ants and spider-hunting wasps that hunt by smell, though it does not smell like its model ant.
facts.cite: Uma D, Durkee C, Herzner G, Weiss M (2013) Double deception: ant-mimicking spiders elude both visually- and chemically-oriented predators. PLoS ONE 8: e79660
facts.kp: Peckhamia does not chemically resemble its model ants
facts.note: Reduced aggression from sphecid wasps and from the model ant; its cuticular hydrocarbons are lower than those of ants and non-mimic spiders. Mechanism unresolved.

facts.t: The ant mimic Peckhamia picata was eaten by predatory salticids less than a third as often as non-mimic jumping spiders.
facts.cite: Durkee CA, Weiss MR, Uma DB (2011) Ant mimicry lessens predation on a North American jumping spider by larger salticid spiders. Environmental Entomology 40: 1223-1231
facts.kp: mimetic jumping spiders were consumed less than a third as often as nonmimetic jumping spiders
facts.note: Model ant Camponotus nearcticus. Supports Batesian mimicry.

facts.t: Phaeacius neither stalks nor invades webs: it sits camouflaged on tree trunks and lunges down on passing insects.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Hallas SEA (1986) Predatory versatility and intraspecific interactions of spartaeine jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae): Brettus adonis, B. cingulatus, Cyrba algerina, and Phaeacius sp. indet. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 13: 491-520
facts.kp: a highly eucryptic, sedentary ambushing specialist that sat on tree trunks and lunged downward
facts.note: Studied species was Phaeacius sp. indet. from Sri Lanka; Jackson (1990) NZ J Zool 17: 491-498 (doi 10.1080/03014223.1990.10422948) found P. malayensis also an ambusher, 'particularly proficient at catching moths and salticids'.

facts.t: Phaeacius malayensis prefers spiders to insects, and other jumping spiders to other hunting spiders.
facts.cite: Li D (2000) Prey preferences of Phaeacius malayensis, a spartaeine jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae) from Singapore. Canadian Journal of Zoology 78: 2218-2226
facts.kp: preferred spiders ... to insects; ... preferred salticids to hunting spiders
facts.note: Preferences held in two of three test types; some depended on a matching (concealing) background.

facts.t: Phidippus audax freezes at low-pitched sounds, and its brain neurons respond to them from over 3 m away, with no eardrums.
facts.cite: Shamble PS, Menda G, Golden JR, Nitzany EI, Walden K, Beatus T, Elias DO, Cohen I, Miles RN, Hoy RR (2016) Airborne acoustic perception by a jumping spider. Current Biology 26: 2913-2920
facts.kp: Responses persisted even when the distances between spider and stimulus source exceeded 3 m
facts.note: 80 Hz tones at ~65 dB SPL; hairs on the foreleg patella likely involved. Cell Press open archive.

full.where: Shamble - 2016 - Airborne Acoustic Perception by a Jumping Spider.txt, Summary (PDF p. 2) and Highlights
full.kp: these animals respond to low-frequency sounds (80 Hz; 65 dB SPL) by freezing

facts.t: Phidippus regius can recognise individual spiders, losing interest in one it has met but re-engaging when shown a new one.
facts.cite: Dahl CD, Cheng Y (2025) Individual recognition in a jumping spider (Phidippus regius). eLife 13: RP97146
facts.kp: indicating the ability to tell apart spiders' identities
facts.checked: read abstract on PubMed (PMID 41217805) and Europe PMC
facts.note: Habituation-dishabituation test; authors infer long-term memory. A non-social species.

facts.t: Phidippus regius has been recorded eating frogs and anole lizards in Florida, more often than any other jumping spider.
facts.cite: Nyffeler M, Zamani A, Cutler B, Krysko KL (2025) Jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) attacking and eating vertebrates: an update. Journal of Arachnology 53: 143-149
facts.where: abstract (and abstract of Nyffeler, Edwards & Krysko 2017 J Arachnol 45: 238-241)
facts.kp: only salticid species in which vertebrate consumption has been reported numerous times
facts.checked: read abstracts on Europe PMC (2025 update and 2017 paper)
facts.note: Prey (Hyla, Osteopilus, Anolis carolinensis, A. sagrei) named in the 2017 abstract. 2017 paper: P. regius is one of the largest salticids, max body length 2.2 cm. 2017 paper doi 10.1636/joa-17-011.1 (DOIs from Crossref).

facts.t: Moving retinae in salticid principal eyes were first described in Phidippus and Metaphidippus: saccades, tracking and scanning.
facts.cite: Land MF (1969) Movements of the retinae of jumping spiders (Salticidae: Dendryphantinae) in response to visual stimuli. Journal of Experimental Biology 51: 471-493
facts.kp: Four types of eye-movements are observed. These are spontaneous activity, saccades, tracking and scanning.
facts.note: Abstract names 'Phidippus and Metaphidippus spp.'. 'First described' is my framing of this 1969 landmark; owner may prefer 'were described by Land (1969) in...'. Scanning includes torsional rotation of the retinae through about 50 degrees. Dropped alternative: Menda et al. 2014 Curr Biol (doi 10.1016/j.cub.2014.09.029), first neural recordings from a salticid brain (P. audax).

facts.t: The green sheen on Phidippus johnsoni chelicerae comes from a stack of 86 alternating air and chitin layers acting as a reflector.
facts.cite: Ingram AL, Deparis O, Boulenguez J, Kennaway G, Berthier S, Parker AR (2011) Structural origin of the green iridescence on the chelicerae of the red-backed jumping spider, Phidippus johnsoni (Salticidae: Araneae). Arthropod Structure & Development 40: 21-25
facts.kp: a stack of 86 layers ... identified as air and chitin respectively
facts.note: Colour restricted to the dorsal paturon.

facts.t: Phidippus audax can be raised from spiderling to adult on dead prey alone, though survival is lower than on live prey.
facts.cite: Vickers ME, Robertson MW, Watson CR, Wilcoxen TE (2014) Scavenging throughout the life cycle of the jumping spider, Phidippus audax (Hentz) (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 42: 277-283
facts.kp: P. audax can survive solely on a diet of dead prey

facts.t: Flies were half the prey of Philaeus chrysops in Azerbaijan, yet 15% of its catches were longer than the spider itself.
facts.cite: Huseynov EF (2008) Natural prey of the jumping spider Philaeus chrysops (Araneae: Salticidae) in different types of microhabitat. Bulletin of the British Arachnological Society 14: 262-268
facts.kp: Diptera ... half of the total prey (50.2%) ... large prey exceeding the length of the spiders
facts.note: Prey ranged 8.1-266.7% of spider length. Generalist: ten arthropod orders.

facts.t: Psecas chapoda supplied 18% of the nitrogen of its host bromeliad, and plants with spiders grew leaves 15% longer.
facts.cite: Romero GQ, Mazzafera P, Vasconcellos-Neto J, Trivelin PCO (2006) Bromeliad-living spiders improve host plant nutrition and growth. Ecology 87: 803-808
facts.kp: contributed 18% of the total nitrogen of its host plant in a greenhouse experiment
facts.note: Host Bromelia balansae; abstract calls it the first study showing nutrient provisioning in a spider-plant system. 18% figure is from a greenhouse experiment, 15% leaf length from a one-year field experiment.

facts.t: Psecas chapoda lives almost only on the bromeliad Bromelia balansae across a large geographic range in South America.
facts.cite: Romero GQ (2006) Geographic range, habitats, and host plants of bromeliad-living jumping spiders (Salticidae). Biotropica 38: 522-530
facts.kp: almost exclusively one bromeliad species over a large geographic range (e.g., Psecas chapoda

facts.t: Its bromeliad host sheltered Psecas chapoda from a wildfire, and the spider population was back to pre-fire levels in 5 months.
facts.cite: de Omena PM, Kersch-Becker MF, Antiqueira PAP, Bernabé TN, Benavides-Gordillo S, Recalde FC, Vieira C, Migliorini GH, Romero GQ (2018) Bromeliads provide shelter against fire to mutualistic spiders in a fire-prone landscape. Ecological Entomology 43: 389-393
facts.kp: returning to pre-fire levels in 5 months
facts.note: Full author list confirmed on Crossref. Fact begins with 'Its' - card can read 'Bromelia balansae sheltered Psecas chapoda...' if preferred.

facts.t: Pseudeuophrys lanigera jumps mainly with its long third legs and needs adhesive claw tufts to avoid slipping on smooth surfaces.
facts.cite: Goetzke HH, Federle W (2021) Role of legs and foot adhesion in salticid spiders jumping from smooth surfaces. Journal of Comparative Physiology A 207: 165-177
facts.kp: P. lanigera accelerated mainly with their long third legs
facts.note: Ablating claw tufts made accelerating spiders slip. Compared with Sitticus pubescens (now Attulus pubescens), which pushes with its fourth legs.

facts.t: The zebra spider Salticus scenicus slows its stalk progressively as it closes on motionless prey.
facts.cite: Dill LM (1975) Predatory behavior of the zebra spider, Salticus scenicus (Araneae: Salticidae). Canadian Journal of Zoology 53: 1284-1289
facts.kp: The zebra spider's stalk velocity declines progressively as it nears its (stationary) prey
facts.note: Also: it turns toward prey seen by the lateral eyes once the prey subtends more than 5.5 degrees, and only moving objects trigger turning.

facts.t: In Salticus scenicus, book lungs or tracheae alone can meet resting oxygen needs, but peak activity needs both working together.
facts.cite: Schmitz A, Perry SF (2001) Bimodal breathing in jumping spiders: morphometric partitioning of the lungs and tracheae in Salticus scenicus (Arachnida, Araneae, Salticidae). Journal of Experimental Biology 204: 4321-4334
facts.kp: high oxygen demands can be met only if both respiratory systems are working together
facts.note: Morphometric estimate, not a direct measurement.

facts.t: Sarinda marcosi is a Batesian mimic of the carpenter ant Camponotus mus; a predatory salticid never caught one in trials.
facts.cite: Hagopián D, Aisenberg A, Laborda Á, Simó M (2021) Morphological and behavioral traits associated with myrmecomorphy in Sarinda marcosi Piza, 1937 (Araneae: Salticidae: Sarindini). Journal of Arachnology 48: 262-271
facts.kp: S. marcosi is a Batesian mimic and C. mus serves as its model
facts.note: Predator was Aphirape flexa (no successful attacks on S. marcosi, n = 15). Study from Uruguay.

facts.t: Female Siler semiglaucus prefer males whose abdomen pattern has lower contrast, judging differences in proportion, as Weber's law predicts.
facts.cite: Kwek BZW, Zhou W, Yu L, Ding G, Li D (2023) Female preference for males with lower pattern contrast follows Weber's law of proportional processing in jumping spiders. Functional Ecology 37: 2434-2446
facts.kp: S. semiglaucus female preference for males with lower pattern contrast follows Weber's law
facts.note: Authors: females used both absolute and proportional differences. DOI from Crossref.

facts.t: Siler collingwoodi is an imperfect ant mimic: its gait matches several ant models and its colours help it blend into the background.
facts.cite: Zeng H, Zhao D, Zhang Z, Gao H, Zhang W (2023) Imperfect ant mimicry contributes to local adaptation in a jumping spider. iScience 26: 106747
facts.kp: a combination of mimicry and camouflage in S. collingwoodi
facts.note: Also had lower predation risk than non-mimetic salticids in assays.

facts.t: Spartaeus spinimanus and S. thailandicus build large sheet webs on tree trunks and catch prey, especially moths, on or near them.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Pollard SD (1990) Web-building and predatory behaviour of Spartaeus spinimanus and Spartaeus thailandicus, primitive jumping spiders (Araneae, Salticidae) from South-east Asia. Journal of Zoology 220: 561-567
facts.kp: build large sheet webs on tree trunks and they capture prey—especially moths
facts.note: Also: captured moths more than flies, and caught both more readily with their webs than without; walk with unusual palp and leg waving.

facts.t: Stenaelurillus guttiger and S. modestus eat almost only termites, and where they meet they specialise on different termite genera.
facts.cite: Pekár S, Petráková Dušátková L, Michálek O, Haddad CR (2020) Coexistence of two termite-eating specialists (Araneae). Ecological Entomology 45: 1307-1317
facts.kp: At the sites where they co-occur, the two species specialise on different termite prey
facts.note: South Africa. S. modestus mainly took Odontotermes.

facts.t: Most species long called Thiodina were moved to Colonus and Nilakantha in 2015, once Thiodina's type species proved unrelated to them.
facts.cite: Bustamante AA, Maddison WP, Ruiz GRS (2015) The jumping spider genus Thiodina Simon, 1900 reinterpreted, and revalidation of Colonus F.O.P.-Cambridge, 1901 and Nilakantha Peckham & Peckham, 1901. Zootaxa 4012(1) (pages not checked)
facts.kp: the type species is not closely related to the more familiar species
facts.note: Simon characterised the genus from species other than the type he designated. Taxonomic; useful context for iNat users who see old 'Thiodina' IDs.

full.where: Maddison 2015, p. 239, Tribe Gophoini, Remarks (secondary support only: cites Bustamante et al. 2015)
full.kp: the discovery that the name Thiodina had long been misapplied

facts.t: Toxeus magnus mothers secrete milk droplets from the epigastric furrow, and spiderlings drink it until the subadult stage.
facts.cite: Chen Z, Corlett RT, Jiao X, Liu S-J, Charles-Dominique T, Zhang S, Li H, Lai R, Long C, Quan R-C (2018) Prolonged milk provisioning in a jumping spider. Science 362: 1052-1055
facts.kp: spiderlings ingest nutritious milk droplets secreted from the mother's epigastric furrow until the subadult stage
facts.checked: read abstract on PubMed (PMID 30498127); abstract does not name the species, confirmed as Toxeus magnus in Jiang et al. 2024 iScience full text (Europe PMC), which cites it as 'the lactating jumping spider Toxeus magnus'
facts.note: An ant-mimic; some sources list it under Myrmarachne in older literature. Check WSC combination.

facts.t: In Toxeus magnus, maternal care continues after offspring reach sexual maturity, a pattern otherwise known from long-lived vertebrates.
facts.cite: Chen Z, Corlett RT, Jiao X, Liu S-J, Charles-Dominique T, Zhang S, Li H, Lai R, Long C, Quan R-C (2018) Prolonged milk provisioning in a jumping spider. Science 362: 1052-1055
facts.kp: Maternal care, as for some long-lived vertebrates, continues after the offspring reach maturity.
facts.note: 'otherwise known from' slightly paraphrases 'as for some long-lived vertebrates'.

facts.t: Toxeus magnus mothers that raised and nursed young outlived both virgin females and mated females that gave no care.
facts.cite: Jiang C, Wang Y-R, Jiao X, Liu J-X, Chen Z (2024) Offspring nursing extends mother's longevity in a long-term maternal cared spider. iScience 27: 110098
facts.kp: mothers who cared for offspring ... lived the longest compared to virgins
facts.checked: read abstract on PubMed (PMID 38947527) and full text on Europe PMC (PMC11214317)

facts.t: Tutelina similis is an ant mimic that also feeds on ants.
facts.cite: Wing K (1983) Tutelina similis (Araneae: Salticidae): an ant mimic that feeds on ants. Journal of the Kansas Entomological Society 56: 55-58
facts.kp: an ant mimic that feeds on ants
facts.checked: title only (Europe PMC record); text not seen
facts.note: Only the title was checked; no DOI or online copy found; owner may want the paper before approving.

facts.t: Yllenus arenarius lives about two years (up to 770 days), the longest wild salticid lifespan known when reported in 2005.
facts.cite: Bartos M (2005) The life history of Yllenus arenarius (Araneae, Salticidae): evidence for sympatric populations isolated by the year of maturation. Journal of Arachnology 33: 214-221
facts.kp: about 720 days for males and 750 days for females (maximum 770 days)
facts.note: Abstract calls it the longest lifespan reported for a salticid under natural conditions (as of 2005). Dune species from Poland.

facts.t: Yllenus arenarius forms two groups at one site, one breeding in odd years and one in even years, with little or no gene flow between.
facts.cite: Bartos M (2005) The life history of Yllenus arenarius (Araneae, Salticidae): evidence for sympatric populations isolated by the year of maturation. Journal of Arachnology 33: 214-221
facts.kp: produces young in odd years, while the other group reproduces in even years
facts.note: 'no or limited gene flow' is the author's inference from lifespan and phenology, not genetic data.

facts.t: Yllenus arenarius burrows into loose dune sand and spins silk nests just below the surface for nights, moults, eggs and winter.
facts.cite: Bartos M (2002) The sub-sand nests of Yllenus arenarius (Araneae, Salticidae): structure, function and construction behavior. Journal of Arachnology 30: 275-280
facts.kp: after burrowing in loose sand
facts.checked: read abstract on BioOne (via WebFetch; tool summarised, short quote only)
facts.note: Four nest types: egg-laying, moulting, overwintering and nocturnal (most common). Juveniles build far more nests than adults.

facts.t: Zygoballus rufipes males come in two discrete sizes, apparently because they mature at two different instars.
facts.cite: Faber DB (1994) Przibram's Rule and male body-size dimorphism in Zygoballus rufipes (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Zoology 232: 191-198
facts.kp: suggesting that males matured at two different instars
facts.note: Females monomorphic. Author consistent with two size-based alternative life-history strategies.

facts.t: A female Cosmophasis in north Queensland was photographed eating butterfly eggs, tugging each one loose with her fangs and palps.
facts.cite: Donovan B, Hill DE (2017) Report of Cosmophasis feeding on butterfly eggs in Queensland (Araneae: Salticidae: Chrysillini). Peckhamia 149.1: 1-3
facts.kp: seized one of the eggs with its fangs, then pulled on that egg
facts.note: Species unconfirmed: the authors suggest a light female of C. thalassina (males at the same site) or C. obscura. Eggs of an unidentified nymphalid; four eggs eaten. Observed in Townsville (town not named in the fact).
facts.file: Donovan and Hill - 2017 - Cosmophasis Feeding on Butterfly Eggs in Queensland.txt

facts.t: Queensland Portia fimbriata raid Euryattus leaf nests even if reared without ever meeting one; other Portia populations and species do not.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Wilcox RS (1990) Aggressive mimicry, prey-specific predatory behaviour and predator-recognition in the predator-prey interactions of Portia fimbriata and Euryattus sp., jumping spiders from Queensland. Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology 26: 111-119
facts.kp: Portia other than P. fimbriata (Q) never adopted this predatory tactic
facts.note: Two findings merged: lab-reared spiders kept from Euryattus behaved like field ones (p. 118: 'was unnecessary for the expression of this predatory tactic'), and P. fimbriata from the Northern Territory and Sri Lanka, P. africana, P. labiata and P. schultzi never did it. Only adults and subadults raid; the raider waits by the leaf's opening, in tests for 28-107 min, and grabs the female as she emerges (p. 114). Complements Portia-4.

facts.t: Young Euryattus spin theridiid-like space webs on rock ledges; adult females hang rolled leaves instead, and adult males build no nest.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1985) The biology of Euryattus sp. indet., a web-building jumping spider (Araneae, Salticidae) from Queensland: utilization of silk, predatory behaviour and intraspecific interactions. Journal of Zoology, London (B) 1: 145-173
facts.kp: Adult males spin neither webs nor suspension nests.
facts.note: Euryattus sp. indet. from north-east Queensland rainforest. Jackson first mistook the juvenile webs for those of small theridiids (p. 168).
facts.file: Jackson - 1985 - Biology of Euryattus - Silk, Predatory Behaviour and Interactions.txt

facts.t: A Queensland Euryattus often leaps 8-10 body lengths onto prey, even snatching insects in flight, but almost never from close range.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1985) The biology of Euryattus sp. indet., a web-building jumping spider (Araneae, Salticidae) from Queensland: utilization of silk, predatory behaviour and intraspecific interactions. Journal of Zoology, London (B) 1: 145-173
facts.kp: Euryattus often made accurate leaps of 8-10 body lengths, sometimes on to insects in flight
facts.note: Euryattus sp. indet. Leaps under three body lengths almost never occurred; the spider backed away first if needed.
facts.file: Jackson - 1985 - Biology of Euryattus - Silk, Predatory Behaviour and Interactions.txt

facts.t: Euryattus egg sacs are flat and papery; Jackson took the first he found for ground spider sacs until young salticids emerged.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1985) The biology of Euryattus sp. indet., a web-building jumping spider (Araneae, Salticidae) from Queensland: utilization of silk, predatory behaviour and intraspecific interactions. Journal of Zoology, London (B) 1: 145-173
facts.kp: he assumed they were gnaphosid egg sacs, until juvenile salticids were seen dispersing from them
facts.note: Euryattus sp. indet. 'Ground spider' = Gnaphosidae. Up to seven sacs found in one suspended leaf (p. 154).
facts.file: Jackson - 1985 - Biology of Euryattus - Silk, Predatory Behaviour and Interactions.txt

facts.t: Cocalus gibbosus prefers moths, creeping up slowly and lunging from about half a body length rather than leaping from afar.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1990) Predatory and nesting behaviour of Cocalus gibbosus, a spartaeine jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae) from Queensland. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 17(4): 483-490
facts.kp: Experiments showed that C. gibbosus prefers moths to other prey.
facts.note: In 22 paired tests it ate the moth but not the fly in 12, the reverse in 3. Lunge usually from about half a body length; leaps of up to 50 mm were rare.
facts.file: Jackson - 1990 - Predatory and Nesting Behaviour of Cocalus gibbosus.txt

facts.t: When Jackson studied Cocalus gibbosus in 1990, just one specimen was on record; he found only five in seven years of Queensland fieldwork.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1990) Predatory and nesting behaviour of Cocalus gibbosus, a spartaeine jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae) from Queensland. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 17(4): 483-490
facts.kp: Only five specimens were found in nature during a 7-year period.
facts.note: The one prior record was an adult male. All field specimens were on rainforest tree trunks. The paper was the first behavioural study of any Cocalus.
facts.file: Jackson - 1990 - Predatory and Nesting Behaviour of Cocalus gibbosus.txt

facts.t: Cocalus gibbosus studs its egg sac with tiny tufts of dense white silk, like the egg sacs of Portia, Cyrba and other spartaeines.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1990) Predatory and nesting behaviour of Cocalus gibbosus, a spartaeine jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae) from Queensland. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 17(4): 483-490
facts.where: p. 484, Oviposition and nesting; p. 488, Discussion (Egg-sacs)
facts.kp: C. gibbosus' egg-sac was always covered by white "spots".
facts.note: Shared with Brettus, Cyrba, Gelotia, Phaeacius and Portia; C. gibbosus puts on especially many spots and a denser cover, perhaps because it leaves its sac in the open.
facts.file: Jackson - 1990 - Predatory and Nesting Behaviour of Cocalus gibbosus.txt

facts.t: In Sri Lanka, Gelotia lanka females were found resting on dead leaves hung inside other spiders' vacant webs, not in webs of their own.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1990) Predatory and silk utilisation behaviour of Gelotia sp. indet. (Araneae: Salticidae: Spartaeinae), a web-invading aggressive mimic from Sri Lanka. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 17(4): 475-482
facts.where: p. 477, Nesting and oviposition; p. 480, Discussion
facts.kp: they appear to prefer to put their leaves in other spiders' webs
facts.note: Studied as an undescribed Gelotia close to G. syringopalpis; only two adult females studied. The host webs were non-sticky domes, apparently pholcid. Refines Gelotia-2 (leaf hanging): it uses others' webs instead of building one. Named only as 'Gelotia sp. indet.' in this 1990 paper; Jackson & Pollard (1996, Annu. Rev. Entomol. 41, p. 295), citing this paper, call the species Gelotia lanka.

facts.t: Gelotia lanka sometimes stabs a web spider and lets it flee, watching it until paralysis sets in, then goes to collect it.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1990) Predatory and silk utilisation behaviour of Gelotia sp. indet. (Araneae: Salticidae: Spartaeinae), a web-invading aggressive mimic from Sri Lanka. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 17(4): 475-482
facts.where: p. 479, Predation by invading alien webs
facts.kp: Stabbed spiders ran away, then became paralysed.
facts.note: Studied as an undescribed Gelotia close to G. syringopalpis. Portia fimbriata does the same (Jackson & Blest 1982, p. 277). Named only as 'Gelotia sp. indet.' in this 1990 paper; Jackson & Pollard (1996, Annu. Rev. Entomol. 41, p. 295), citing this paper, call the species Gelotia lanka.

facts.t: Gelotia lanka stalks web spiders from the web's edge, keeping its hind legs on a twig and plucking the silk, for up to 4 hours.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1990) Predatory and silk utilisation behaviour of Gelotia sp. indet. (Araneae: Salticidae: Spartaeinae), a web-invading aggressive mimic from Sri Lanka. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 17(4): 475-482
facts.where: p. 479, Predation by invading alien webs; p. 480, Discussion
facts.kp: Sometimes it remained at the web edge for as long as 2-4 h.
facts.note: Studied as an undescribed Gelotia close to G. syringopalpis. In this it is more like Brettus, Cocalus and Cyrba than Portia, which goes right into the web. Named only as 'Gelotia sp. indet.' in this 1990 paper; Jackson & Pollard (1996, Annu. Rev. Entomol. 41, p. 295), citing this paper, call the species Gelotia lanka.

facts.t: The first Portia fimbriata Jackson and Blest met in the field looked so like debris that it was pushed aside with a finger until it moved.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Blest AD (1982) The biology of Portia fimbriata, a web-building jumping spider (Araneae, Salticidae) from Queensland: utilization of webs and predatory versatility. Journal of Zoology, London 196: 255-293
facts.kp: it was not recognized but was casually pushed aside with a finger
facts.note: North-east Queensland rainforest. Its rest posture hides the outline of body and legs among debris in webs.
facts.file: The biology of Portia fimbriata, a webbuilding jumping spider (Araneae, Salticidae) from Queensland - utilization of webs and predatory.txt

facts.t: Web invasion is risky for Portia fimbriata: two were found dead in theridiid webs, and one lost three legs yet still caught the theridiid.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Blest AD (1982) The biology of Portia fimbriata, a web-building jumping spider (Araneae, Salticidae) from Queensland: utilization of webs and predatory versatility. Journal of Zoology, London 196: 255-293
facts.kp: Web invasion was evidently risky for the invader.
facts.note: Field observations, north-east Queensland. The theridiid fed on one of the lost legs before the Portia caught and ate it.
facts.file: The biology of Portia fimbriata, a webbuilding jumping spider (Araneae, Salticidae) from Queensland - utilization of webs and predatory.txt

facts.t: Dropped onto a web complex of about 30 social uloborids, Portia fimbriata spiderlings had killed every one by the end of the day.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Blest AD (1982) The biology of Portia fimbriata, a web-building jumping spider (Araneae, Salticidae) from Queensland: utilization of webs and predatory versatility. Journal of Zoology, London 196: 255-293
facts.kp: By the end of the day, there were no living uloborids remaining.
facts.note: First-instar spiderlings from a field-collected egg case, placed on a uloborid (Philoponella) web complex in the field near Cairns; only one spiderling was caught by a uloborid. Spiderlings already pluck and lure like adults.
facts.file: The biology of Portia fimbriata, a webbuilding jumping spider (Araneae, Salticidae) from Queensland - utilization of webs and predatory.txt

facts.t: In the field, every Portia fimbriata that first scanned the scene got to the web; none of the 30 that skipped scanning did.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Wilcox RS (1993) Observations in nature of detouring behaviour by Portia fimbriata, a web-invading aggressive mimic jumping spider from Queensland. Journal of Zoology, London 230: 135-139
facts.kp: but all Portia that did scan reached the web
facts.note: Field tests near Cairns with captive adult females released below webs. Scanning before setting off lasted 6-137 min (median 23.5 min).
facts.file: Observations in nature of detouring behaviour by Portia fimbriata, a web-invading aggressive mimic jumping spider from Queensland.txt

facts.t: Paracyrba wanlessi, not known to deceive web spiders, failed an island escape test that seven aggressive-mimic spartaeines solved.
facts.cite: Cross FR, Carvell GE, Jackson RR, Grace RC (2020) Arthropod intelligence? The case for Portia. Frontiers in Psychology 11: 568049
facts.where: pp. 9-10, Solving a novel confinement problem; Fig. 8
facts.kp: there was no evidence of the two non-aggressive-mimic species solving the same novel problem
facts.note: Review; original Cross & Jackson (2015), the same study behind Cocalus-3 (Cocalus gibbosus also failed). Solvers: Portia africana, P. schultzi, Brettus adonis, B. albolimbatus, Cyrba algerina, C. ocellata, C. simoni.
facts.file: Arthropod Intelligence - The Case for Portia.txt

facts.t: Myrmarachne lupata often taps an insect with its forelegs, as ants tap with their antennae, and then lunges at it rather than leaping.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1986) The biology of ant-like jumping spiders (Araneae, Salticidae): prey and predatory behaviour of Myrmarachne with particular attention to M. lupata from Queensland. Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society 88: 179-190
facts.kp: Attacking by lunging instead of leaping and the pronounced use of pre-attack tapping
facts.note: Spiders from Cairns, north Queensland. Jackson notes tapping alerts the prey yet still works, and keeps the ant-like look; males never leapt on prey.
facts.file: The biology of antlike jumping spiders (Araneae, Salticidae) - prey and predatory behaviour of Myrmarachne with particular attention to M.txt

facts.t: Myrmarachne lupata chews into other spiders' silk nests to eat their eggs; males can rip a nest open with their long fangs.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1986) The biology of ant-like jumping spiders (Araneae, Salticidae): prey and predatory behaviour of Myrmarachne with particular attention to M. lupata from Queensland. Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society 88: 179-190
facts.kp: also preys on the eggs of other spiders which it extracts from their nests
facts.note: Laboratory; nests of Bavia aericeps, Helpis minitabunda, Trite planiceps and Clubiona. It salivates on the silk while chewing. Long male fangs sometimes got stuck in the silk.
facts.file: The biology of antlike jumping spiders (Araneae, Salticidae) - prey and predatory behaviour of Myrmarachne with particular attention to M.txt

facts.t: Male Myrmarachne lupata, whose long jaws tend to startle prey, caught winged flies on 11% of attempts, against 44% for females.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1986) The biology of ant-like jumping spiders (Araneae, Salticidae): prey and predatory behaviour of Myrmarachne with particular attention to M. lupata from Queensland. Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society 88: 179-190
facts.kp: the lesser success rate of males compared to females
facts.note: 18 attempts by males, 25 by females (P < 0.05). Males caught only one moth in all tests, but sometimes caught a second fly while holding the first in their jaws.
facts.file: The biology of antlike jumping spiders (Araneae, Salticidae) - prey and predatory behaviour of Myrmarachne with particular attention to M.txt

facts.t: Eight Myrmarachne species watched feeding in the wild in Australia, Africa and Asia were eating various insects, but none was eating ants.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1986) The biology of ant-like jumping spiders (Araneae, Salticidae): prey and predatory behaviour of Myrmarachne with particular attention to M. lupata from Queensland. Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society 88: 179-190
facts.kp: Eight species were observed feeding, in nature, in Australia, Kenya, Malaysia and Sri Lanka
facts.note: Prey included flies, mosquitoes, bugs, a katydid, a moth and a lacewing. Australian species: M. lupata, M. striatipes and two unidentified species (Queensland). Supports Batesian, not aggressive, mimicry. Some species tapped ants briefly, then walked away.
facts.file: The biology of antlike jumping spiders (Araneae, Salticidae) - prey and predatory behaviour of Myrmarachne with particular attention to M.txt

facts.t: Four Myrmarachne species living together in north Queensland each mimic a different ant: Opisthopsis, Polyrhachis, Tetraponera, green ants.
facts.cite: Ceccarelli FS (2008) Behavioral mimicry in Myrmarachne species (Araneae, Salticidae) from North Queensland, Australia. Journal of Arachnology 36(2): 344-351
facts.kp: Paired photographs of Myrmarachne mimics and their respective model ant species from Townsville
facts.note: Undescribed species sp. A, B, D, F (separated by DNA, Ceccarelli & Crozier 2007): models Opisthopsis haddoni, Polyrhachis nr obtusa, Tetraponera punctulata, Oecophylla smaragdina. Each spider was collected within 5 m of a colony of its model. One campus site in Townsville.
facts.file: Ceccarelli - 2008 - Behavioral Mimicry in Myrmarachne from North Queensland.txt

facts.t: The ant-eating Chalcotropis gulosus prefers ants with their jaws full, whatever they carry, and so picks long-jawed Myrmarachne males too.
facts.cite: Nelson XJ, Jackson RR (2006) Compound mimicry and trading predators by the males of sexually dimorphic Batesian mimics. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 273: 367-372
facts.where: p. 367, Abstract; p. 370, Results (Tables 3-5); p. 371, Discussion
facts.kp: C. gulosus chose safer encumbered ants in preference to more dangerous unencumbered ants
facts.note: Philippine species; lab-reared spiders with no prior experience of ants, tested with lures. Parcel could be a fly, a beetle or part of another ant. It did not distinguish Myrmarachne males from laden ants. Companion to Myrmarachne-1 (same paper).
facts.file: Nelson and Jackson - Compound Mimicry and Trading Predators in Myrmarachne.txt

facts.t: In tests, every Habronattus trimaculatus attacked then rejected crickets laced with bitter quinine, while every Phidippus regius ate them.
facts.cite: Vickers ME, Heisey ML, Taylor LA (2021) Alternative responses by two species of jumping spiders to unpalatability and toxicity in prey. Journal of Arachnology 49(3): 324-331
facts.where: p. 324, Abstract; p. 328, Results and Discussion
facts.kp: all H. trimaculatus attacked and rejected them while all P. regius attacked and consumed
facts.note: Florida spiders. Also applies to Phidippus regius. Toxic springtails in the diet cut growth in both, apparently more in H. trimaculatus. The authors speculate that toxin sensitivity may have driven Habronattus's red-filter colour vision (see Habronattus-1).
facts.file: Vickers - Alternative Responses by Two Jumping Spider Species to Unpalatability and Toxicity in Prey.txt

facts.t: Evarcha culicivora stalked stick-figure images of a blood-fed Anopheles even with the parts scattered, but not if their angles changed.
facts.cite: Dolev Y, Nelson XJ (2014) Innate pattern recognition and categorization in a jumping spider. PLoS ONE 9(6): e97819
facts.where: p. 1, Abstract; pp. 2-4, Results and Discussion
facts.kp: the otherwise identical set of elements was no longer perceived as prey
facts.note: Lab-reared spiders (at least second generation); juveniles had never met mosquitoes. Projected video stimuli. The authors conclude the angle between elements, not the whole outline, identifies the prey.
facts.file: Dolev and Nelson - Innate Pattern Recognition and Categorization in a Jumping Spider.txt

facts.t: Resting overnight, Evarcha arcuata spiderlings had bouts of retinal movement and leg twitching about every 17 minutes, like REM sleep.
facts.cite: Rößler DC, Kim K, De Agrò M, Jordan A, Galizia CG, Shamble PS (2022) Regularly occurring bouts of retinal movements suggest an REM sleep-like state in jumping spiders. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 119(33): e2204754119
facts.kp: Periodic bouts of retinal movements in spiderlings were clearly visible
facts.note: Spiderlings 1-9 days old still have unpigmented, see-through cuticle, so the moving retinal tubes can be filmed. Bouts lasted a median 77 s at median 17-min intervals, both lengthening through the night; leg curls always came with retinal movement. Adults showed the same twitch and leg-curl rhythm. The authors compare bout length with REM in rats.
facts.file: Regularly occurring bouts of retinal movements suggest an REM sleep-like state in jumping spiders.txt

facts.t: Euryattus from a site without Portia rarely evaded or fought off a stalking Portia fimbriata, unlike Euryattus living alongside it.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Pollard SD (1996) Predatory behavior of jumping spiders. Annual Review of Entomology 41: 287-308
facts.where: p. 295, Coevolution of P. fimbriata and Euryattus sp.
facts.kp: only rarely evaded or attacked stalking P. fimbriata
facts.note: Review; original Jackson & Wilcox (1993) Predator-prey co-evolution of Portia fimbriata and Euryattus sp., jumping spiders from Queensland. Mem. Qld Mus. 33: 557-560. Lab-reared spiders; the Portia-free population was about 15 km away, and Portia hunted it more efficiently. Taken as evidence of coevolution. Builds on Euryattus-3.

facts.t: Male Myrmaplata plataleoides have no venom openings in their huge fangs, so they pin prey down and stab it repeatedly instead.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Pollard SD (1996) Predatory behavior of jumping spiders. Annual Review of Entomology 41: 287-308
facts.kp: but the male's fangs have no openings
facts.note: Review uses the older name Myrmarachne plataleoides (now Myrmaplata plataleoides). Original Pollard (1994) Consequences of sexual selection on feeding in male jumping spiders. J. Zool. Lond. 234. Male chelicerae are about five times the female's length; many prey escape, and males feed more slowly, but they eat eggs as well as females do.

facts.t: With its long jaws, a male Myrmaplata plataleoides looks like a weaver ant major worker carrying a minor worker between nests.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Pollard SD (1996) Predatory behavior of jumping spiders. Annual Review of Entomology 41: 287-308
facts.kp: with chelicerae that simulate the minor worker, closely resembles this duo
facts.note: Review uses Myrmarachne plataleoides. This is the reviewers' interpretation (majors carry minors by the abdomen between subnests). Species-specific case of the 'encumbered ant' idea in Myrmarachne-1. Juvenile males have short chelicerae; the long ones appear at the final moult (Mathew 1954, cited p. 301).

facts.t: Simaetha in colonies of the social spider Phryganoporus candidus avoid its sticky silk by keeping to vegetation and old, unsticky silk.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Pollard SD (1996) Predatory behavior of jumping spiders. Annual Review of Entomology 41: 287-308
facts.where: p. 297, Predatory versatility in nonspartaeine web-building salticids
facts.kp: moving carefully along vegetation and old, no-longer-sticky silk
facts.note: Review; original Jackson (1985) The biology of Simaetha paetula and S. thoracica, web-building jumping spiders from Queensland. J. Zool. Lond. B 1: 175-210. The cribellate silk does stick to them; this is how they avoid becoming the social spiders' prey. Tropical Queensland.

facts.t: Plexippus paykulli wraps its tube nest in a sticky tangle of silk that holds insects such as grasshoppers long enough for it to attack.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Pollard SD (1996) Predatory behavior of jumping spiders. Annual Review of Entomology 41: 287-308
facts.where: p. 297, Predatory versatility in nonspartaeine web-building salticids
facts.kp: tend to become stuck for several seconds, or even minutes
facts.note: Review; original Jackson & Macnab (1989), NZ J. Zool. (on P. paykulli display, mating and predation). The spider leaps onto stuck insects from the nest or walks across the silk to them. The review uses it to show the blurry line between nest and web.

facts.t: Pellenes arciger of southern France spins a large silk sheet in vegetation, probably as a prey-catching web.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Pollard SD (1996) Predatory behavior of jumping spiders. Annual Review of Entomology 41: 287-308
facts.where: p. 297, Predatory versatility in nonspartaeine web-building salticids
facts.kp: builds a large silk sheet in the vegetation
facts.note: Review; original Lopez (1986) Construction de toiles en 'voile de bateau' par une araignée salticide languedocienne. Bull. Soc. Arch. Béziers. The review says predatory use 'has not been studied' and calls the web probably a prey-capture device. 'Low' is my word; the review says 'in the vegetation': drop 'low' if preferred.

facts.t: Zenodorus orbiculatus often waits head-down on ant-infested tree trunks and lunges down on passing ants instead of chasing them.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Pollard SD (1996) Predatory behavior of jumping spiders. Annual Review of Entomology 41: 287-308
facts.where: p. 298, Prey-specific predatory behavior of ant-eating salticids
facts.kp: frequently positions itself facing down on ant-infested tree trunks
facts.note: Review calls it 'Zendora (formerly Pystira) orbiculata' (a typo for Zenodorus); current name Zenodorus orbiculatus. Original Jackson & van Olphen (1991) Prey-capture techniques and prey-preferences of Corythalia canosa and Pystira orbiculata, ant-eating jumping spiders. J. Zool. Lond. 223: 577-591. Unlike the other ant-eaters reviewed, it attacks ants from almost any direction. Complements Zenodorus-2 (abstract-only).

facts.t: Phyaces comosus, a minute, cryptic jumping spider from Sri Lanka, enters other spiders' nests and eats the eggs one at a time.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Pollard SD (1996) Predatory behavior of jumping spiders. Annual Review of Entomology 41: 287-308
facts.kp: a minute, highly cryptic salticid from Sri Lanka
facts.note: Review; original Jackson (1986) The biology of Phyaces comosus. Bull. Br. Mus. Nat. Hist. (Zool.) 50: 109-116. Small Myrmarachne juveniles use the same tactic. Donovan & Hill 2017 (p. 1) add that Moffett (1991) photographed ~2 mm Phyaces comosus eating eggs and young in a guarded Epeus brood.

facts.t: Phidippus stalks caterpillars to 10-12 mm and pins the head, but leaps at flies from 25-30 mm away, biting near the wing bases.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Pollard SD (1996) Predatory behavior of jumping spiders. Annual Review of Entomology 41: 287-308
facts.where: pp. 298-299, Subtle predatory versatility in Phidippus
facts.kp: stalking closer to caterpillars than to flies before attacking
facts.note: Review; originals Edwards & Jackson (1993, 1994). Stated for 'Phidippus spp.' studied in North America; the review calls these two prey-specific strategies.

facts.t: Phidippus clarus can eavesdrop on the courtship signals of Schizocosa wolf spiders and use them to hunt the courting spiders.
facts.cite: Nelson XJ (2025) Cognition in spiders: small brains on eight legs gain traction. Journal of Zoology 326: 93-108
facts.kp: Phidippus clarus jumping spiders can use eavesdropping to hunt courting Schizocosa ocreata wolf spiders
facts.note: Review (Thomas Henry Huxley Review); original Roberts et al. (2007). The review does not say which signal channel (visual or vibratory) the spider uses. DOI taken from the download stamp on each page.
facts.file: Cognition in spiders - Small brains on eight legs gain traction.txt

facts.t: Male Portia fimbriata catch jumping spiders less well than females as their big palps give them away; with palps removed they did as well.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Pollard SD (1996) Predatory behavior of jumping spiders. Annual Review of Entomology 41: 287-308
facts.kp: his enlarged palps reveal him as a predator to his visually competent prey
facts.note: Queensland population, where Portia hunts salticids by cryptic stalking with palps tucked (see Portia-2). The palp-removal result is unpublished data (Pollard & Jackson) reported in this review. Juvenile males, with enlarged palps but no male markings, were also less effective.

facts.t: Juvenile Evarcha culicivora creep up behind a mosquito, crawl under it and bite its thorax, riding it in flight until the venom works.
facts.cite: Aguilar-Arguello S, Nelson XJ (2021) Jumping spiders: an exceptional group for comparative cognition studies. Learning & Behavior 49: 276-291
facts.kp: approaching the mosquito from behind, creeping under it, and biting underneath the thorax
facts.note: Review; original Nelson, Jackson & Sune (2005) on Anopheles-specific prey capture by small juveniles of E. culicivora, J. Arachnol. 33: 541-548. Innate; adults just pounce, being heavy enough to stop the mosquito flying off. 'Resting' is implied by the approach from behind; the review does not say it explicitly.
facts.file: Jumping spiders - An exceptional group for comparative cognition studies.txt

facts.t: In Kenya, Menemerus tropicus lives in nest complexes, its silk nests built side by side and on top of one another.
facts.cite: Aguilar-Arguello S, Nelson XJ (2021) Jumping spiders: an exceptional group for comparative cognition studies. Learning & Behavior 49: 276-291
facts.kp: built side-by-side and on top of one another
facts.note: Review; original Jackson (1986b). The review calls it 'remarkably social'; most Menemerus, including other Kenyan species in similar habitats, are not.
facts.file: Jumping spiders - An exceptional group for comparative cognition studies.txt

facts.t: Marpissa muscosa raised with siblings did better in learning tasks than siblings raised alone.
facts.cite: Aguilar-Arguello S, Nelson XJ (2021) Jumping spiders: an exceptional group for comparative cognition studies. Learning & Behavior 49: 276-291
facts.kp: reared in social environments outperform their siblings reared in isolation in learning tasks
facts.note: Review; original Liedtke & Schneider (2017). Social rearing seemed to matter more than physical enrichment (tentative). Nelson 2025 (Cognition in spiders, p. 99) adds that M. muscosa can relearn reversed colour-reward associations.
facts.file: Jumping spiders - An exceptional group for comparative cognition studies.txt

facts.t: Abracadabrella's rear end seems to mimic a fly's head: two black mounds pass for compound eyes and the spinnerets for mouthparts.
facts.cite: Richardson BJ, Whyte R, Żabka M (2025) A key to the genera of Australian jumping spiders, factsheet Abracadabrella. Lucid
facts.kp: resembling the compound eyes of a fly
facts.note: Field guide p. 225 says the same in less detail (mounds "appearing to mimic the eyes of a large fly").

facts.t: Abracadabrella walks backwards, wiping its front end with its front legs the way a fly cleans its wings.
facts.cite: Richardson BJ, Whyte R, Żabka M (2025) A key to the genera of Australian jumping spiders, factsheet Abracadabrella. Lucid
facts.kp: the spider walks backwards, wiping its cephalothorax with its front legs
facts.note: Field guide p. 225 also notes the backward walk.

facts.t: Afraflacilla rubs tubercles on its leg femora against tubercles on the sides of the carapace, making sounds to signal its own species.
facts.cite: Whyte R, Anderson G (2017) A field guide to spiders of Australia. CSIRO Publishing, Clayton South VIC. ISBN 9780643107076 (paperback)
facts.where: p. 227, caption to Afraflacilla stridulator (genus statement "They all stridulate")
facts.kp: are rubbed against the tubercles on the side of the
facts.checked: read Salticidae chapter pp. 222-307 and salticid captions elsewhere (owner's copy, text extract)
facts.note: Existing Afraflacilla-1 only says the group has stridulatory organs; this adds how they work. p. 226 says the sounds are used in courtship and possibly defence. The guide's Afraflacilla courti is now Psenuc courti (factsheet Psenuc).
facts.file: A field guide to spiders of Australia.txt

facts.t: Arasia are extremely fast runners; A. mollicoma is common on tree trunks, especially pale-trunked gum trees.
facts.cite: Whyte R, Anderson G (2017) A field guide to spiders of Australia. CSIRO Publishing, Clayton South VIC. ISBN 9780643107076 (paperback)
facts.kp: especially on pale-trunked gum trees
facts.checked: read Salticidae chapter pp. 222-307 and salticid captions elsewhere (owner's copy, text extract)

facts.t: Astia hariola lives under dark or burnt bark and on the ground in eucalypt forest and woodland, and can be locally abundant.
facts.cite: Richardson BJ, Whyte R, Żabka M (2025) A key to the genera of Australian jumping spiders, factsheet Astia. Lucid
facts.kp: Found under dark or burnt bark and on the ground in eucalypt forests
facts.note: Factsheet says Astia has one described Australian species, A. hariola. Field guide p. 229: very common under bark in dry to wet woodland.

facts.t: Heliophanus has no Australian species: Karsch's 1878 Heliophanus maculatus from Australia appears to be Astia hariola.
facts.cite: Richardson BJ, Whyte R, Żabka M (2025) A key to the genera of Australian jumping spiders, factsheet Astia. Lucid
facts.kp: removing Heliophanus from the Australian fauna
facts.note: Also usable for Astia. The factsheet credits the figure to Wesolowska (1986). The Salticidae overview sheet also lists Heliophanus among names no longer used in Australia.

facts.t: Female Astilodes mariae are pale to translucent, well camouflaged among rainforest greenery; males are more colourful.
facts.cite: Whyte R, Anderson G (2017) A field guide to spiders of Australia. CSIRO Publishing, Clayton South VIC. ISBN 9780643107076 (paperback)
facts.kp: The female in particular is pale to translucent, well

facts.t: Bavia aericeps, found from Malaysia to Australia and on several Pacific islands, is a powerful jumper able to leap a metre.
facts.cite: Whyte R, Anderson G (2017) A field guide to spiders of Australia. CSIRO Publishing, Clayton South VIC. ISBN 9780643107076 (paperback)
facts.kp: prodigious jumper, able to jump a metre

facts.t: Bianor maculatus often gathers in groups: one pair shared a fence with eight other males and eight females, and no other spiders.

facts.t: Clynotis severus ('severe') is named for the lines on its carapace, which give it a glowering, frowning look.

facts.t: Coccorchestes ferreus, a beetle mimic of Cape York rainforest, walks like a beetle rather than like a spider.
facts.cite: Richardson BJ, Whyte R, Żabka M (2025) A key to the genera of Australian jumping spiders, factsheet Coccorchestes. Lucid
facts.kp: It walks in a beetle-like rather than spider-like fashion.
facts.note: Biology paragraph speaks of "this beetle mimic"; C. ferreus is the only Australian species. Field guide p. 234: all Coccorchestes species (New Guinea and north) mimic beetles.

facts.t: Copocrossa tenuilineata is extremely elongate: the male's front legs are longer than its whole body.
facts.cite: Whyte R, Anderson G (2017) A field guide to spiders of Australia. CSIRO Publishing, Clayton South VIC. ISBN 9780643107076 (paperback)
facts.kp: the male's front legs longer than its body
facts.checked: read Salticidae chapter pp. 222-307 and salticid captions elsewhere (owner's copy, text extract)
facts.note: Factsheet: Copocrossa is not closely related to any other Australian genus, and only the female has been formally described.
facts.file: A field guide to spiders of Australia.txt

facts.t: Cosmophasis lami, known from Fiji, turns up in Australian ports and on the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, likely spread by people.
facts.cite: Richardson BJ, Whyte R, Żabka M (2025) A key to the genera of Australian jumping spiders, factsheet Cosmophasis. Lucid
facts.kp: Cosmophasis lami from Fiji is found in Australia in ports
facts.note: Ports named are Darwin and Townsville. Field guide p. 236 also says it is probably being spread by humans.

facts.t: Male Cosmophasis, especially C. thalassina, drum the surface they stand on with their palps.
facts.cite: Richardson BJ, Whyte R, Żabka M (2025) A key to the genera of Australian jumping spiders, factsheet Cosmophasis. Lucid
facts.kp: drum the substrate with their pedipalps
facts.note: Field guide p. 222 likens the C. thalassina male drumming on its leaf to a tabla player, as a courtship signal; p. 24 says male Cosmophasis tap legs and palps in complicated rhythms.

facts.t: Cosmophasis bitaeniata builds its retreats on the same plants as its green tree ant hosts: the more ants, the more spider retreats.
facts.cite: Whyte R, Anderson G (2017) A field guide to spiders of Australia. CSIRO Publishing, Clayton South VIC. ISBN 9780643107076 (paperback)
facts.kp: The more Green Tree Ants there are, the more spider retreats there will be.
facts.checked: read Salticidae chapter pp. 222-307 and salticid captions elsewhere (owner's copy, text extract)
facts.note: Existing Cosmophasis-1/-2 cover the chemical mimicry. The guide also says it avoids adult ants during daylight.
facts.file: A field guide to spiders of Australia.txt

facts.t: Damoetas shares its name with a cattle herder in the pastoral verses of the ancient Greek poet Theocritus.
facts.cite: Whyte R, Anderson G (2017) A field guide to spiders of Australia. CSIRO Publishing, Clayton South VIC. ISBN 9780643107076 (paperback)
facts.kp: Damoetas was the name of a Greek cattle herder.

facts.t: In Damoetas nitidus ('gleaming'), a shiny double band on the abdomen suggests three body segments, aiding its ant mimicry.

facts.kp: double band around the abdomen which enhances the mimicry by suggesting three body

facts.t: Euryattus wallacei courts with an elaborate sequence of front-leg movements reminiscent of semaphore.

facts.t: Euryattus ventralis, a New Guinea species, was first recorded in Australia from two females collected on Cape York in 2016.

facts.kp: the first recorded Australian specimen of this species normally found in PNG

facts.t: Females of a north Queensland Frewena have fluffy palps, very unusual in jumping spiders, and may wave them in courtship.
facts.cite: Whyte R, Anderson G (2017) A field guide to spiders of Australia. CSIRO Publishing, Clayton South VIC. ISBN 9780643107076 (paperback)
facts.kp: Fluffy palps in the female are extremely unusual for Jumping Spiders.

facts.t: Frigga crocuta, of a South American genus, has spread across Pacific islands to New Caledonia, the Coral Sea and Torres Strait.

facts.kp: Frigga crocuta has extended its range across the Pacific to Australia

facts.t: Grayenulla's long third legs evolved independently of Maratus's; males don't wave them in courtship but may display fluffy palps.

facts.t: Hasarius adansoni is a tramp species of warm port cities, and in cooler countries turns up in hothouses.
facts.cite: Richardson BJ, Whyte R, Żabka M (2025) A key to the genera of Australian jumping spiders, factsheet Hasarius. Lucid
facts.kp: It is a tramp species often occurring around port cities.
facts.note: Factsheet spells it adansonii; existing facts use adansoni. Field guide p. 247: common in most of the world's cities, often in houses.

facts.t: Helpis minitabunda is New Zealand's only Helpis, and its New Zealand name, Bronze Aussie Jumper, has spread back to Australia.
facts.cite: Whyte R, Anderson G (2017) A field guide to spiders of Australia. CSIRO Publishing, Clayton South VIC. ISBN 9780643107076 (paperback)
