facts.checked: read the genus notes in full (owner's copy; OCR text of the second scan)
facts.note: Secondary: Davies & Żabka summarising Jackson (1986c), who found three mating tactics depending on the female's maturity and location (away from nest, in nest, subadult in nest). Compare existing Mopsus-1.
facts.file: Davies 1989 Illustrated Keys to the genera of jumping spiders in Aus 2.txt

facts.t: Frigga crocuta, a large spider introduced to Australia, was known there in 1989 only from Simon's old types of 'Sandalodes calvus'.
facts.cite: Davies VT, Żabka M (1989) Illustrated keys to the genera of jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) in Australia. Memoirs of the Queensland Museum 27(2): 189-266
facts.where: p. 246, key couplet and notes under Frigga; Appendix
facts.kp: of which no fresh material has been collected
facts.checked: read the genus notes in full (owner's copy; OCR text of the second scan)
facts.note: Key marks Frigga '(introduced)'. Galiano (1979) synonymised Sandalodes calvus Simon with F. crocuta; the appendix gives the calvus syntypes (MNHN Paris) as from north-east Queensland.
facts.file: Davies 1989 Illustrated Keys to the genera of jumping spiders in Aus 2.txt

facts.t: In Ohilimia the trochanter of leg I is nearly as long as the femur, in effect an extra segment that greatly extends the front legs' reach.
facts.cite: Hill DE, Ng Y (2025) Standing display of the Australasian jumping spider Ohilimia (Araneae: Salticidae: Euophryini: Papuaphryni). Peckhamia 326.1: 1-12
facts.kp: represents in effect an additional segment altogether, quite as long as the femur
facts.note: Also true of the closely related Diolenius (same paper). Peckhamia usually has no DOI.
facts.file: Hill and Ng - 2025 - Standing Display of Ohilimia.txt

facts.t: Ohilimia was said to mimic a fly by walking backwards with its front legs held like wings, but a 2025 video study saw no backward walking.
facts.cite: Hill DE, Ng Y (2025) Standing display of the Australasian jumping spider Ohilimia (Araneae: Salticidae: Euophryini: Papuaphryni). Peckhamia 326.1: 1-12
facts.where: p. 1 (quoting Davies & Zabka 1989 on O. scutellata) and p. 11, 'Role of the standing display'
facts.kp: we did not observe this behavior in Ohilimia
facts.note: The 2025 study filmed a single male (Ohilimia sp., North Maluku, Indonesia), so absence of backward walking is weak evidence; the authors also question why a salticid would mimic a fly. The original claim (Davies & Zabka 1989) was made for O. scutellata in north Queensland, then placed in Diolenius. See the conflicts entry for Diolenius-1.
facts.file: Hill and Ng - 2025 - Standing Display of Ohilimia.txt

facts.t: A filmed male Ohilimia, standing still, raised and lowered its long front legs once or twice a second while flicking them at about 10 Hz.
facts.cite: Hill DE, Ng Y (2025) Standing display of the Australasian jumping spider Ohilimia (Araneae: Salticidae: Euophryini: Papuaphryni). Peckhamia 326.1: 1-12
facts.where: p. 9 (summary of results) and Figs 5 and 10
facts.kp: elevation of the trochanter (at cycles of ~1-2 Hz) and elevation of the femur
facts.note: One male of an unidentified Ohilimia species from Indonesia; the authors call it a standing (advertisement) display, not courtship, and its palps alternated at about 2 Hz. Courtship of Ohilimia is undescribed.
facts.file: Hill and Ng - 2025 - Standing Display of Ohilimia.txt

facts.t: Maratus avibus and M. caeruleus can produce viable hybrids: a hybrid male sired young, but hybrid-by-hybrid pairs laid no eggs.
facts.cite: Otto JC, Hill DE (2019) Catalogue of the Australian peacock spiders (Araneae: Salticidae: Euophryini: Maratus, Saratus), version 3. Peckhamia 148.3: 1-28
facts.kp: Mating by M. avibus with M. caeruleus can result in viable hybrids.
facts.note: Laboratory crosses. The hybrid male mated with a female M. caeruleus that laid eggs and produced juveniles; two hybrid females mated to hybrid males laid no eggs.
facts.file: Otto and Hill - 2019 - Catalogue of Australian Peacock Spiders - Version 3.txt

facts.t: Male Maratus jactatus punctuate their fan dance with a sideways jolt of the whole body lasting only 20 to 30 milliseconds.
facts.cite: Otto JC, Hill DE (2015) Two new peacock spiders of the calcitrans group from southern Queensland (Araneae: Salticidae: Euophryinae: Maratus). Peckhamia 121.1: 1-34
facts.where: p. 9, 'Male courtship display', and p. 15, Fig. 16 (1000 fps video)
facts.kp: rapid jolting or rocking movement of the whole body that lasts for only 20-30msec
facts.note: The jolt follows a quick return of the extended leg III behind the tilted fan, repeated at about 1-3 per second; the name jactatus means rocking or jolting (p. 1). Popularly 'Sparklemuffin' (Otto & Hill 2019 catalogue).
facts.file: Otto and Hill - 2015 - Two New Peacock Spiders of the Calcitrans Group.txt

facts.t: Across 21 Maratus species, male colour patterns had image statistics unlike natural scenes, while females' patterns matched them.
facts.cite: Hardenbicker M-C, Schubert J, Tedore C (2025) A comparison of image statistics of peacock jumping spider colour patterns and natural scenes. Ecology and Evolution 15: e71363
facts.where: Abstract, p. 1 of the article (reproduced as Appendix II of Schubert's 2025 thesis, thesis p. 286)
facts.kp: We find that the image statistics of male patterns diverge from those of natural scenes
facts.checked: read abstract and introduction (published article reproduced in owner's copy of the thesis)
facts.note: Peer-reviewed, open access. Authors read it as males evolving conspicuous patterns and females camouflage. Spectral slope measured from multispectral images, compared with photos of leaf litter and sticks like the spiders' habitat (taken in Sweden and Queensland). The intro notes an earlier finding that M. spicatus prefers natural-scene statistics, as humans seem to.

facts.t: Mantispid larvae coil round the waist of female Maratus scutulatus and ride with her to her egg sac, where they eat the eggs.
facts.cite: Otto JC, Hill DE, Whyte R (2019) Australian jumping spiders of the genus Hypoblemum (Araneae: Salticidae: Euophryini). Peckhamia 180.1: 1-62
facts.kp: a mantispid larva coiled around the pedicel of the female
facts.note: Published as Hypoblemum scutulatum; Hypoblemum was synonymised with Maratus by Otto & Hill (2021/2022, per Schubert 2025), so the current name is Maratus scutulatus (Schubert's 2025 thesis would resurrect Hypoblemum, but that is unpublished). The caption says the larvae were common in one New South Wales population and cites Hill 2011 for the egg-feeding.
facts.file: Otto, Hill and Whyte - 2019 - Australian Jumping Spiders of the Genus Hypoblemum.txt

facts.t: Several fimbriatus-group Maratus, including M. volpei and M. playa, live on salt lakes; at least six more salt-lake species await names.
facts.cite: Schubert J (2025) Integrative systematics of the Australian peacock spiders and their allies. PhD thesis, University of Sydney
facts.where: p. 198, Chapter V, Salinatus remarks; also p. 13-14 (Chapter II introduction)
facts.kp: at least six additional undescribed species are known from salt lake systems
facts.note: Thesis, not peer-reviewed; Chapter V is 'prepared for submission' to Invertebrate Systematics. The thesis moves these species to a new genus Salinatus, a name not available under the ICZN until published, so Maratus is used. Published species: M. volpei Schubert 2020 (Zootaxa 4758: 1-44), M. ammophilus Otto & Hill 2022, M. playa Otto & Hill 2023. Chapter II (accepted in Zootaxa) adds M. furnus ('oven'), seen hunting in large numbers on a salt-lake surface in WA.

facts.t: Maratus volans ('flying') was so named because Pickard-Cambridge was told it flew on its flaps; a 1970 guide still thought it might fly.
facts.cite: Otto JC, Hill DE (2019) Catalogue of the Australian peacock spiders (Araneae: Salticidae: Euophryini: Maratus, Saratus), version 3. Peckhamia 148.3: 1-28
facts.kp: Pickard-Cambridge (1874) was told that this spider used its flaps to fly
facts.note: The 1970 guide is Mascord's Australian Spiders in Colour; Pickard-Cambridge also guessed the flaps had a 'sexual' function, and a British Museum guide to flying animals (Ridewood 1912/1913) figured the species.
facts.file: Otto and Hill - 2019 - Catalogue of Australian Peacock Spiders - Version 3.txt

facts.t: The Mediterranean Saitis barbipes sits inside an otherwise Australian radiation, which points to dispersal rather than Gondwanan break-up.
facts.cite: Schubert J (2025) Integrative systematics of the Australian peacock spiders and their allies. PhD thesis, University of Sydney
facts.where: p. 260, Chapter V discussion, 'Biogeography of the Saitis group'
facts.kp: Mediterranean Saitis is nested within an otherwise predominantly Australian radiation
facts.note: Thesis, not peer-reviewed; it corroborates Zhang & Maddison 2013 (Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution 68: 81-92, doi 10.1016/j.ympev.2013.03.017), who argued from divergence dating that vicariance cannot explain the distribution. Citing Zhang & Maddison 2013 would be better once checked. Different from Saitis-3 (Saitis/Maratus paraphyly).

facts.t: Jotus saw no new species for over a century until J. remus was described in 2016; five more followed in 2019.
facts.cite: Schubert J (2025) Integrative systematics of the Australian peacock spiders and their allies. PhD thesis, University of Sydney
facts.kp: The taxonomy of Jotus was stagnant for more than a century until Otto & Hill
facts.note: Thesis, not peer-reviewed (Chapter IV prepared for Zootaxa). The 2016 species is J. remus (Otto & Hill 2016, Peckhamia 133.1); the five 2019 species are in Baehr, Schubert & Harms 2019 ('The Brushed Jumping Spiders'). The thesis also proposes moving three species from Maratus to Jotus and four new Jotus species, all unpublished.

facts.t: Phintella, a mainly Asian genus, was first recorded from Australia in 2012, when P. monteithi was described from north Queensland.
facts.cite: Żabka M (2012) Phlegra Simon, 1876, Phintella Strand 1906 and Yamangalea Maddison, 2009 (Arachnida: Araneae: Salticidae) - new species and new generic records for Australia. Zootaxa 3176: 61-68
facts.kp: Phlegra Simon, Phintella Strand and Yamangalea Maddison are newly recorded from Australia
facts.note: Types from rainforest (beating) and riparian woodland in north Queensland; named for entomologist Geoff Monteith. Phintella otherwise known from eastern and south-eastern Asia, Japan, the Philippines and Indonesia (as of 2012).

facts.t: Before Phlegra proszynskii was found on Lord Howe Island, the genus was known no further east than Vietnam.
facts.cite: Żabka M (2012) Phlegra Simon, 1876, Phintella Strand 1906 and Yamangalea Maddison, 2009 (Arachnida: Araneae: Salticidae) - new species and new generic records for Australia. Zootaxa 3176: 61-68
facts.kp: the localities of Phlegra in Vietnam have been the eastern most
facts.note: Described in 2012 from a single female collected on a cliff face in 1971. Zabka flags its placement as provisional: unlike other Phlegra it has fissidentate cheliceral teeth and one-chambered spermathecae, so a male is needed to confirm the genus. Lord Howe Island is part of New South Wales (also named in existing fact Ancipitilobus-1).

facts.t: Before 2021, the spider now called Cytaea asper had carried four species names across eight genera, from Attus to Zenodorus.
facts.cite: Trębicki L, Patoleta BM, Dabert M, Żabka M (2021) Redescription of type species of the genus Cytaea Keyserling, 1882 (Araneae: Salticidae) - an integrative approach. The European Zoological Journal 88(1): 933-947
facts.where: pp. 943-944, Cytaea asper synonymy list; p. 945, Discussion
facts.kp: Ascyltus asper, Cytaea severa and C. barbatissima were transferred and synonymized as Cytaea asper
facts.note: Names in the synonymy: Attus asper Karsch 1878, Euryattus senex Simon 1885, Zenodorus asper, Ascyltus asper, Hasarius barbatissimus Keyserling 1881, Servaea barbatissima, Cytaea barbatissima, Plexippus severus Thorell 1881 and Cytaea severa (genera: Attus, Euryattus, Zenodorus, Ascyltus, Hasarius, Servaea, Plexippus, Cytaea). Some synonymies (e.g. Euryattus senex) predate this paper. Open access. Check the current spelling on WSC (asper vs aspera, as Cytaea is feminine).
facts.file: Redescription of type species of the genus Cytaea Keyserling, 1882 (Araneae - Salticidae) - an integr.txt

facts.t: Tomocyrba of East Africa and Madagascar resembles Gorgopsina of Eocene Baltic amber and has been called a possible survivor of that fauna.
facts.cite: Żabka M (1988) Fossil Eocene Salticidae (Araneae) from the collection of the Museum of Earth in Warsaw. Annales Zoologici 41(13): 415-420
facts.where: p. 418 (Gorgopsina frenata remarks) and references (Proszynski & Zabka 1983)
facts.kp: indicate the already mentioned affinity with the East African and Madagascan genus Tomocyrba
facts.note: 'Hypothetic survivor of the Amber fauna' is the title of Proszynski & Zabka 1983 (Acta Zoologica Cracoviensia 26: 563-578), cited here; that paper would be the better source if available. Zabka also notes Baltic amber salticids resemble today's Oriental and African faunas. Old scan; text read via OCR.
facts.file: Fossil Eocene Salticidae (Araneae) from the collection of the Muzeum of Earth in Warsaw.txt

facts.t: In 1976 Prószyński based Plexippoides on a Japanese spider but made an Iranian species its type, as its type specimen was easiest to get.
facts.cite: Prószyński J (1984) Remarks on Anarrhotus, Epeus and Plexippoides (Araneae, Salticidae). Annales Zoologici 37(16): 399-410
facts.kp: then the only species with the type easily available
facts.note: The genus was based on study of Plexippus annulipedis (Japan); the type species chosen was Yllenus starmuehlneri Roewer 1955 (Iran), which Prószyński later saw as an outlier at the edge of the genus' range. Check that P. starmuehlneri remains the type species on WSC. Old scan; text read via OCR.
facts.file: Remarks on Anarrhotus, Epeus and Plexippoides (Araneae, Salticidae).txt

facts.t: Papuaneon tualapa, a large, hairy Neon look-alike, was described from just two specimens collected in 2008 in Papua New Guinea.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2016) Papuaneon, a new genus of jumping spiders from Papua New Guinea (Araneae: Salticidae: Neonini). Zootaxa 4200(3): 437-443
facts.kp: These are the only two specimens known.
facts.note: One male and one female, forest interior and riverside at 1000-1100 m, Southern Highlands Province, found on Hewa land during a 2008 biodiversity survey.
facts.file: Maddison - 2016 - Papuaneon, a new genus of jumping spiders from Papua New Guinea (Araneae - Salticidae - Neonini).txt

facts.t: Female Papuaneon tualapa have swollen, bright white palp tips, so that they look like subadult males.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2016) Papuaneon, a new genus of jumping spiders from Papua New Guinea (Araneae: Salticidae: Neonini). Zootaxa 4200(3): 437-443
facts.kp: Palp: tarsus swollen, as if a subadult male.
facts.note: Based on the single known female (paratype); its palp tibia and tarsus are bright white with long white setae. Not checked whether later-described Australian Papuaneon females share this.
facts.file: Maddison - 2016 - Papuaneon, a new genus of jumping spiders from Papua New Guinea (Araneae - Salticidae - Neonini).txt

facts.t: Beltian bodies were 91% of food items Bagheera kiplingi was seen eating in Mexico but 60% in Costa Rica, where it took more animal prey.
facts.cite: Meehan CJ, Olson EJ, Reudink MW, Kyser TK, Curry RL (2009) Herbivory in a spider through exploitation of an ant-plant mutualism. Current Biology 19(19): R892-R893
facts.where: p. R892, main text and Fig. 1B
facts.kp: nearly the full diet of spiders in Mexico (91% of items consumed)
facts.note: Field observation counts of food items, 2001-2008. Extracted text interleaves other Current Biology items; only the spider article used. PII S0960-9822(09)01626-1 printed; DOI not printed.

facts.t: Hundreds of Bagheera kiplingi can live on one ant-acacia; a 7-year Costa Rican survey found only two on any other kind of plant.
facts.cite: Meehan CJ, Olson EJ, Reudink MW, Kyser TK, Curry RL (2009) Herbivory in a spider through exploitation of an ant-plant mutualism. Current Biology 19(19): R892-R893
facts.kp: Hundreds of individual B. kiplingi may inhabit a single ant-acacia
facts.note: Survey: 1174 salticids of 48 species at the Costa Rican site; only two B. kiplingi seen off Vachellia. Also >200 nests, all on ant-acacias or adjacent foliage.

facts.t: Bagheera kiplingi builds its nests at the tips of older acacia leaves, the parts of the plant its guard ants patrol least.
facts.cite: Meehan CJ, Olson EJ, Reudink MW, Kyser TK, Curry RL (2009) Herbivory in a spider through exploitation of an ant-plant mutualism. Current Biology 19(19): R892-R893
facts.kp: generally build their nests at the distal tips of older leaves
facts.note: 86% of 110 nests; low ant-patrol rates of those leaves are documented in the paper's Supplemental Data.

facts.t: The Beltian bodies that Bagheera kiplingi lives on are about 80% structural fibre, a poor stand-in for animal prey.
facts.cite: Meehan CJ, Olson EJ, Reudink MW, Kyser TK, Curry RL (2009) Herbivory in a spider through exploitation of an ant-plant mutualism. Current Biology 19(19): R892-R893
facts.kp: these low-fat food bodies are 80% structural fiber
facts.note: The 80% figure is cited by Meehan et al. from Heil et al. 2004 (Chemoecology 14: 45-52). Authors suggest the spider's digestion may be specialised for this fibrous, nitrogen-poor food.

facts.t: In Phidippus audax, brain neurons that respond to airborne sound also fired when one long hair on a front leg was vibrated directly.
facts.cite: Shamble PS, Menda G, Golden JR, Nitzany EI, Walden K, Beatus T, Elias DO, Cohen I, Miles RN, Hoy RR (2016) Airborne acoustic perception by a jumping spider. Current Biology 26: 1-8 (in-press pagination as printed in this copy, 7 November 2016)
facts.where: Summary (PDF p. 2) and Fig. 4; hair on patella of leg I
facts.kp: stimulation of hairs on the patella of the foreleg was sufficient to generate responses
facts.note: Authors conclude air-flow-sensitive hairs are the likely sound detectors. Copy shows in-press pagination 1-8; final journal page range not printed (check via DOI).
facts.file: Shamble - 2016 - Airborne Acoustic Perception by a Jumping Spider.txt

facts.t: Phidippus audax is most sensitive to sounds near 80 Hz, a range that overlaps the wingbeat tones of spider-hunting wasps.
facts.cite: Shamble PS, Menda G, Golden JR, Nitzany EI, Walden K, Beatus T, Elias DO, Cohen I, Miles RN, Hoy RR (2016) Airborne acoustic perception by a jumping spider. Current Biology 26: 1-8 (in-press pagination as printed in this copy, 7 November 2016)
facts.where: Discussion, 'Behavioral Relevance of Sound' (pp. 5-6 of in-press copy)
facts.kp: well suited to detecting acoustic signals generated by potentially dangerous flying insects
facts.note: Wasp link is the authors' interpretation (flying hymenopterans ~100 Hz dominant frequency); keep wording as overlap, not proven function.
facts.file: Shamble - 2016 - Airborne Acoustic Perception by a Jumping Spider.txt

facts.t: Plexippus petersi and P. paykulli told three ant species apart by sight alone, rarely giving aggressive red weaver ants a long look.
facts.cite: Vijayan S, Casiker C, Uma D (2018) Look before you jump: jumping spiders discriminate different ants by visual cues. bioRxiv preprint 349696 (posted 18 June 2018; not peer reviewed)
facts.kp: Spiders barely gave long looks to weaver ants compared to golden-back and procession ants.
facts.note: PREPRINT (bioRxiv, not peer reviewed). Spiders from Bengaluru, India; ants behind a clear barrier (no touch or scent). Results pooled for the two Plexippus species. With dead, motionless ant lures the spiders no longer discriminated.
facts.file: Vijayan - Look Before You Jump - Jumping Spiders Discriminate Ants by Visual Cues - Preprint.txt

facts.t: Males of eight Portia species were drawn to the airborne scent of their own females and not to that of other species' females.
facts.cite: Nelson XJ, Warui CM, Jackson RR (2012) Widespread reliance on olfactory sex and species identification by lyssomanine and spartaeine jumping spiders. Biological Journal of the Linnean Society (2012; volume and pages not printed in this early-view copy)
facts.kp: significantly more males of all species chose the odour of conspecific females
facts.note: Species: P. africana, albimana, fimbriata (Queensland), jianfengensis, labiata, cf. orientalis, quei, schultzi. Heterospecific choice was another Portia for 7 of them, Spartaeus spinimanus for P. jianfengensis. Females did not respond to male odour. Olfactory pheromones had already been shown in four Portia species (Jackson & Cross 2011).
facts.file: Widespread reliance on olfactory sex and species identification by lyssomanine and spartaeine jumping spiders.txt

facts.t: Male Cocalus gibbosus from Queensland chose the airborne scent of their own females over the scent of female Portia fimbriata.
facts.cite: Nelson XJ, Warui CM, Jackson RR (2012) Widespread reliance on olfactory sex and species identification by lyssomanine and spartaeine jumping spiders. Biological Journal of the Linnean Society (2012; volume and pages not printed in this early-view copy)
facts.kp: significantly more males of all species chose the odour of conspecific females
facts.note: Y-maze olfactometer, scent only (view blocked). 16 of 20 males chose conspecific female odour. Males were also drawn to conspecific female odour in retention tests (Table 3).
facts.file: Widespread reliance on olfactory sex and species identification by lyssomanine and spartaeine jumping spiders.txt

facts.t: Male Gelotia lanka from Sri Lanka found females by airborne scent alone, choosing their own species' odour over Portia labiata's.
facts.cite: Nelson XJ, Warui CM, Jackson RR (2012) Widespread reliance on olfactory sex and species identification by lyssomanine and spartaeine jumping spiders. Biological Journal of the Linnean Society (2012; volume and pages not printed in this early-view copy)
facts.kp: significantly more males of all species chose the odour of conspecific females
facts.note: 16 of 20 males chose conspecific over P. labiata female odour. Females showed no attraction to male odour.
facts.file: Widespread reliance on olfactory sex and species identification by lyssomanine and spartaeine jumping spiders.txt

facts.t: Male Lyssomanes viridis and L. patens told their own species' females from the other's by airborne scent alone.
facts.cite: Nelson XJ, Warui CM, Jackson RR (2012) Widespread reliance on olfactory sex and species identification by lyssomanine and spartaeine jumping spiders. Biological Journal of the Linnean Society (2012; volume and pages not printed in this early-view copy)
facts.kp: significantly more males of all species chose the odour of conspecific females
facts.note: L. patens 27/30 and L. viridis 25/30 males chose own-species female odour. Related to Lyssomanes-3 (pheromones speed visual recognition, Tedore & Johnsen) but a different finding.
facts.file: Widespread reliance on olfactory sex and species identification by lyssomanine and spartaeine jumping spiders.txt

facts.sp: Zenodorus durvillei, Zenodorus metallescens, Zenodorus orbiculatus
facts.t: Three Australian Zenodorus species often stab a large ant and let go, then follow and stab again until it is weak enough to hold.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Li D (2001) Prey-capture techniques and prey preferences of Zenodorus durvillei, Z. metallescens and Z. orbiculatus, tropical ant-eating jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) from Australia. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 28: 299-341
facts.kp: made successive stabbing attacks that noticeably weakened the ant
facts.note: 'Large' = ants about the spider's size or larger; smaller ants and other prey were simply held. Stabbed ants usually ran 10-20 mm away and the spider followed at 10-50 mm. Naming: Zhang & Maddison (2012) merged Zenodorus into Omoedus; the World Spider Catalog still listed Zenodorus separately in 2019 (Szűts et al. 2020, pp. 539-541). Fact keeps the paper's and app's name.

facts.sp: Zenodorus durvillei, Zenodorus metallescens, Zenodorus orbiculatus
facts.t: Three Zenodorus species get stuck on sticky cribellate silk, so to reach ants in such webs they step along trapped debris instead.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Li D (2001) Prey-capture techniques and prey preferences of Zenodorus durvillei, Z. metallescens and Z. orbiculatus, tropical ant-eating jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) from Australia. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 28: 299-341
facts.kp: appears to depend largely on skill at using detritus in the web as a path
facts.note: Webs used included Badumna (cribellate). Contrasts with web-invading spartaeines, to whose cuticle cribellate glue does not adhere. Without a debris path the spiders usually left without attacking. Naming: Zhang & Maddison (2012) merged Zenodorus into Omoedus; the World Spider Catalog still listed Zenodorus separately in 2019 (Szűts et al. 2020, pp. 539-541). Fact keeps the paper's and app's name.

facts.t: Zenodorus durvillei and Z. orbiculatus often nest on dead leaves inside other spiders' webs, but were seen taking only ants there.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Li D (2001) Prey-capture techniques and prey preferences of Zenodorus durvillei, Z. metallescens and Z. orbiculatus, tropical ant-eating jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) from Australia. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 28: 299-341
facts.where: p. 301, 'Use of alien webs as nesting and predation sites in the field'
facts.kp: they were never seen taking any other type of prey from webs
facts.note: Never observed for Z. metallescens. Females, especially with eggs, nested in webs. Lab: two Z. durvillei and one Z. orbiculatus were killed by Badumna candida after missing a leap and landing on the web. Naming: Zhang & Maddison (2012) merged Zenodorus into Omoedus; the World Spider Catalog still listed Zenodorus separately in 2019 (Szűts et al. 2020, pp. 539-541). Fact keeps the paper's and app's name.

facts.sp: Zenodorus durvillei, Zenodorus metallescens, Zenodorus orbiculatus
facts.t: Even with dead, motionless lures, three Zenodorus species picked ants over termites and other insects by sight alone.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Li D (2001) Prey-capture techniques and prey preferences of Zenodorus durvillei, Z. metallescens and Z. orbiculatus, tropical ant-eating jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) from Australia. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 28: 299-341
facts.kp: Even termites, which humans often mistake for ants, were distinguished by the Zenodorus
facts.note: Lures were dead insects without movement cues; also distinguished ants from bugs, cockroaches, crickets, flies, lacewings, mantises, hoppers, psocids and mayflies. Naming: Zhang & Maddison (2012) merged Zenodorus into Omoedus; the World Spider Catalog still listed Zenodorus separately in 2019 (Szűts et al. 2020, pp. 539-541). Fact keeps the paper's and app's name.

facts.t: Simon grouped the flat, bark-dwelling Holoplatys with Marpissa, but DNA puts it in an Australasian clade with the beetle-like Simaetha.
facts.cite: Maddison WP, Bodner MR, Needham KM (2008) Salticid spider phylogeny revisited, with the discovery of a large Australasian clade (Araneae: Salticidae). Zootaxa 1893: 49-64
facts.kp: scatters the astioids among many groups based largely on general body form
facts.note: Simon (1901-1903) placed Holoplatys and Corambis in the Marpissae. Maddison 2015 (p. 243) keeps Holoplatys and Simaetha together in tribe Viciriini (Astioida).

facts.t: DNA unexpectedly showed the ant-like Leptorchestes to be related to ground-dwelling Yllenus and the American desert genus Paramarpissa.
facts.cite: Maddison WP, Bodner MR, Needham KM (2008) Salticid spider phylogeny revisited, with the discovery of a large Australasian clade (Araneae: Salticidae). Zootaxa 1893: 49-64
facts.kp: An unexpected result was the strong support for a relationship among Yllenus
facts.note: Group now tribe Leptorchestini; Maddison 2015 (p. 247) calls it 'unexpected before molecular data'. Paramarpissa described in 2008 as a small tree-bark dweller of the American deserts.

facts.t: A 5.2 mm juvenile Hypaeus from Ecuador was measured jumping 25 cm on level ground, more than 45 times its own body length.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2015) A phylogenetic classification of jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 43(3): 231-292
facts.kp: jump 25 cm on a horizontal surface (more than 45 times its body length)
facts.note: Maddison's own measurement of a juvenile Hypaeus aff. porcatus; not a formal study.
facts.file: Maddison - A Phylogenetic Classification of Jumping Spiders.txt

facts.t: Diplocanthopoda marina, a hasariine jumping spider described in 1925, lives in the intertidal zone.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2015) A phylogenetic classification of jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 43(3): 231-292
facts.where: p. 246, Tribe Hasariini, Remarks; live photo Fig. 100 (Singapore)
facts.kp: Diplocanthopoda marina Abraham, 1925 lives in the intertidal zone
facts.note: Maddison cites Abraham 1925 and his own unpublished data; no further detail given.
facts.file: Maddison - A Phylogenetic Classification of Jumping Spiders.txt

facts.t: Ant-like Peckhamia and Synageles wave their second legs as mock antennae, not the first legs that other ant-like salticids use.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2015) A phylogenetic classification of jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 43(3): 231-292
facts.where: p. 244, Subtribe Synagelina, Remarks; Fig. 68 (Peckhamia sp.)
facts.kp: unusual in waving the second pair of legs like antennae
facts.note: Stated for the ant-like synagelines generally (Synageles, Peckhamia); could also go on a Synageles card.
facts.file: Maddison - A Phylogenetic Classification of Jumping Spiders.txt

facts.t: Agorius, an ant-like jumping spider of Asia and Australasia, holds its first legs curled and raised in life, like antennae.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2015) A phylogenetic classification of jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 43(3): 231-292
facts.kp: Agorius holds the first legs curled and raised in life, like antennae
facts.note: Tribe Agoriini (Agorius, Synagelides); placement within Salticoida uncertain.
facts.file: Maddison - A Phylogenetic Classification of Jumping Spiders.txt

facts.t: Abracadabrella resembles an insect facing backwards, an illusion also seen in Orsima, though Abracadabrella achieves it differently.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2015) A phylogenetic classification of jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 43(3): 231-292
facts.where: p. 254, 'Salticids that look like ants, beetles, and other things'
facts.kp: and in different form in Abracadabrella (Astioida?)
facts.note: Maddison gives no detail of how Abracadabrella's version differs; owner may know the look from the field. Placement in Astioida queried.
facts.file: Maddison - A Phylogenetic Classification of Jumping Spiders.txt

facts.t: Some Asemonea, like Orsima, look like an insect facing backwards, the spinnerets passing for the insect's mouthparts.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2015) A phylogenetic classification of jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 43(3): 231-292
facts.where: p. 254, 'Salticids that look like ants, beetles, and other things'; Fig. 4 (A. tenuipes)
facts.kp: This is indeed convincing, and is replicated in some Asemonea
facts.note: Fig. 4 shows A. tenuipes (male, Singapore). Not stated for all Asemonea.
facts.file: Maddison - A Phylogenetic Classification of Jumping Spiders.txt

facts.t: Beetle-like Coccorchestes has ant-like close relatives such as Sobasina; at least four salticid lineages pair beetle and ant forms.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2015) A phylogenetic classification of jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 43(3): 231-292
facts.where: p. 254, 'Salticids that look like ants, beetles, and other things'
facts.kp: close relatives of the beetle-like forms are ant-like
facts.note: Other pairs: Cylistella/Synemosyna, Pachyballus/Marengo, Sassacus/Bellota. A beetle-like body evolved at least eight times in salticids.
facts.file: Maddison - A Phylogenetic Classification of Jumping Spiders.txt

facts.t: A spider reported as 'Plexippus validus' in eye-ultrastructure studies compiled by Blest and colleagues was really Servaea incana.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2015) A phylogenetic classification of jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 43(3): 231-292
facts.kp: the reported Plexippus validus Urquhart, 1893 is the euophryine Servaea incana
facts.note: Refers to the compilation in Blest et al. 1990 (Cell and Tissue Research 262: 445-460). Means plexippines remain unsampled for principal-eye ultrastructure.
facts.file: Maddison - A Phylogenetic Classification of Jumping Spiders.txt

facts.t: Some Phidippus exceed 20 mm in length, which with their broad, high bodies puts them among the world's largest jumping spiders.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2015) A phylogenetic classification of jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 43(3): 231-292
facts.kp: includes some of the largest salticids in the world, sometimes exceeding 20 mm in length
facts.note: Maddison cites Edwards 2004 for Phidippus.
facts.file: Maddison - A Phylogenetic Classification of Jumping Spiders.txt

facts.t: Eupoa of subtropical South-east Asia are the only known minute leaf-litter dwellers among the early-branching salticid lineages.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2015) A phylogenetic classification of jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 43(3): 231-292
facts.kp: these are the only known minute litter-dwelling non-salticines, resembling Neon or Neonella
facts.note: 'Non-salticines' = salticids outside subfamily Salticinae. Eupoinae described as new in this paper; range given as southern China, Vietnam, Thailand.
facts.file: Maddison - A Phylogenetic Classification of Jumping Spiders.txt

facts.t: Colonus and its gophoine relatives move slowly and deliberately, yet are excellent jumpers that tense hard before popping into long leaps.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2015) A phylogenetic classification of jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 43(3): 231-292
facts.kp: While their motions are often deliberate and slow, they are excellent jumpers
facts.note: Stated for gophoines (formerly 'thiodinines'); Colonus named as the best-known genus. Also notes a carapace-leg stridulatory apparatus and paired bulbous setae on legs I.
facts.file: Maddison - A Phylogenetic Classification of Jumping Spiders.txt

facts.t: Horns on the chelicerae evolved more than once within Padilla, unrelated to habitat, which points to sexual selection.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2015) A phylogenetic classification of jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 43(3): 231-292
facts.kp: convergent evolution of remarkable cheliceral horns in Padilla was uncorrelated with environment
facts.note: Secondary: Maddison summarises Andriamalala (2007), a phylogenetic study not in the library; check the primary source if possible.
facts.file: Maddison - A Phylogenetic Classification of Jumping Spiders.txt

facts.t: Neon, first known from the northern hemisphere, has radiated widely in Australia, and DNA places it in a mainly Australasian group.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2015) A phylogenetic classification of jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 43(3): 231-292
facts.kp: molecular data have placed it in the primarily Australasian Astioida
facts.note: Maddison cites Richardson et al. 2006 and Richardson 2013 for the Australian radiation and Maddison et al. 2008 for the placement. Complements Neon-1 (Neonini/Papuaneon).
facts.file: Maddison - A Phylogenetic Classification of Jumping Spiders.txt

facts.t: Synemosyna, often an excellent mimic of slender Pseudomyrmex ants, is closely related to the beetle-like Cylistella.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2015) A phylogenetic classification of jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 43(3): 231-292
facts.kp: Synemosyna, often an excellent mimic of the elongate ant Pseudomyrmex
facts.note: Neotropical. One of Maddison's four beetle-like/ant-like sister pairings (Cylistella/Synemosyna).
facts.file: Maddison - A Phylogenetic Classification of Jumping Spiders.txt

facts.t: Although Ananeon's name means 'not Neon', Maddison suggested in 2015 that it may belong in Neon's own tribe, Neonini.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2015) A phylogenetic classification of jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 43(3): 231-292
facts.where: p. 242, Tribe Neonini, Monophyly and Diagnosis
facts.kp: The genus Ananeon (Richardson 2013) may be a neonine.
facts.note: Tentative placement ('may be'). Pairs with Ananeon-1 (name means 'not Neon').
facts.file: Maddison - A Phylogenetic Classification of Jumping Spiders.txt

facts.t: Leviea, the only myrmarachnine genus that is not ant-like, has been found only above 2,500 m in the mountains of Papua New Guinea.
facts.cite: Szűts T, Zhang J, Gallé-Szpisjak N, De Bakker D (2020) Jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) of the Papua New Guinean Mount Wilhelm and surrounding mountains. In: Robillard T, Legendre F, Villemant C, Leponce M (eds) Insects of Mount Wilhelm, Papua New Guinea, vol. 2. Mémoires du Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle 214: 521-555. Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris. ISBN 978-2-85653-836-4
facts.kp: Leviea is currently the only non-antlike Myrmarachnini genus
facts.note: Text: 'Leviea always above 2500m in several mountains'. Leviea (subtribe Levieina) was described by Maddison & Szűts 2019. Ant-like Levieina (Papuamyr, Agorioides) were found mainly at 200-1000 m. Not in the library's AU list.
facts.file: Szuts - 2020 - Jumping Spiders of Mount Wilhelm and Surrounding Mountains.txt

facts.t: Vallvonas, a euophryine described in 2020 from the mountains of Papua New Guinea, has a name that is a random combination of letters.
facts.cite: Szűts T, Zhang J, Gallé-Szpisjak N, De Bakker D (2020) Jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) of the Papua New Guinean Mount Wilhelm and surrounding mountains. In: Robillard T, Legendre F, Villemant C, Leponce M (eds) Insects of Mount Wilhelm, Papua New Guinea, vol. 2. Mémoires du Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle 214: 521-555. Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris. ISBN 978-2-85653-836-4
facts.kp: The genus name is a random combination of letters.
facts.note: Monotypic (V. zarandi, named for the first author's son). Holotype from moss forest at about 2800-3000 m. Mount Wilhelm is not named in the fact (locality rule).
facts.file: Szuts - 2020 - Jumping Spiders of Mount Wilhelm and Surrounding Mountains.txt

facts.t: Waymadda, a cocalodine genus described in 2020 from Papua New Guinea, takes its name from the first letters of Wayne Maddison's name.
facts.cite: Szűts T, Zhang J, Gallé-Szpisjak N, De Bakker D (2020) Jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) of the Papua New Guinean Mount Wilhelm and surrounding mountains. In: Robillard T, Legendre F, Villemant C, Leponce M (eds) Insects of Mount Wilhelm, Papua New Guinea, vol. 2. Mémoires du Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle 214: 521-555. Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris. ISBN 978-2-85653-836-4
facts.kp: The generic name is built by concatenating of the first few letters of his name.
facts.note: Includes W. enduwa (new) and W. rufa (Maddison 2009, moved from Tabuina).
facts.file: Szuts - 2020 - Jumping Spiders of Mount Wilhelm and Surrounding Mountains.txt

facts.t: Waymadda enduwa takes its name from the local Kuman name for the mountain summit where it was found.
facts.cite: Szűts T, Zhang J, Gallé-Szpisjak N, De Bakker D (2020) Jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) of the Papua New Guinean Mount Wilhelm and surrounding mountains. In: Robillard T, Legendre F, Villemant C, Leponce M (eds) Insects of Mount Wilhelm, Papua New Guinea, vol. 2. Mémoires du Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle 214: 521-555. Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris. ISBN 978-2-85653-836-4
facts.kp: derived from Enduwa Kombuglu, the local Kuman name of Mt Wilhelm's peak
facts.note: The mountain is Mt Wilhelm, Papua New Guinea; kept unnamed in the fact. Type series from about 1700 m.
facts.file: Szuts - 2020 - Jumping Spiders of Mount Wilhelm and Surrounding Mountains.txt

facts.t: A second Capeyorkia species, C. richardsoni, was described from Papua New Guinea in 2020, along with the genus's first known female.
facts.cite: Szűts T, Zhang J, Gallé-Szpisjak N, De Bakker D (2020) Jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) of the Papua New Guinean Mount Wilhelm and surrounding mountains. In: Robillard T, Legendre F, Villemant C, Leponce M (eds) Insects of Mount Wilhelm, Papua New Guinea, vol. 2. Mémoires du Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle 214: 521-555. Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris. ISBN 978-2-85653-836-4
facts.kp: the female morphology described for the first time
facts.note: Both sexes have reddish scales around the anterior median eyes. Earlier the genus was known only from C. vulpecula of Cape York (see Capeyorkia-1, -2).
facts.file: Szuts - 2020 - Jumping Spiders of Mount Wilhelm and Surrounding Mountains.txt

facts.t: No male Porius was known to science until 2020, when the male of P. decempunctatus from Papua New Guinea was first described.
facts.cite: Szűts T, Zhang J, Gallé-Szpisjak N, De Bakker D (2020) Jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) of the Papua New Guinean Mount Wilhelm and surrounding mountains. In: Robillard T, Legendre F, Villemant C, Leponce M (eds) Insects of Mount Wilhelm, Papua New Guinea, vol. 2. Mémoires du Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle 214: 521-555. Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris. ISBN 978-2-85653-836-4
facts.kp: resulting in the first description of any Porius male morphology
facts.note: Originally described as Ballus decempunctatus (1915), later moved to Coccorchestes and then Porius. Most specimens came from canopy fogging of rainforest trees at about 500-2070 m.
facts.file: Szuts - 2020 - Jumping Spiders of Mount Wilhelm and Surrounding Mountains.txt

facts.t: Omoedus koehalmii, described in 2020 from the mountains of Papua New Guinea, honours the Hungarian stand-up comedian Zoltán Kőhalmi.
facts.cite: Szűts T, Zhang J, Gallé-Szpisjak N, De Bakker D (2020) Jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) of the Papua New Guinean Mount Wilhelm and surrounding mountains. In: Robillard T, Legendre F, Villemant C, Leponce M (eds) Insects of Mount Wilhelm, Papua New Guinea, vol. 2. Mémoires du Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle 214: 521-555. Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris. ISBN 978-2-85653-836-4
facts.kp: The species is dedicated to Zoltán Kőhalmi, Hungarian stand-up comedian and scriptwriter.
facts.note: Genus used in the broad sense of Zhang & Maddison 2012 (including Zenodorus and Pystira); the authors note the dispute (pp. 539-541).
facts.file: Szuts - 2020 - Jumping Spiders of Mount Wilhelm and Surrounding Mountains.txt

facts.t: Males of Omoedus baloghi have been collected both in lowland forest at 200 m and in moss forest near 3,000 m in Papua New Guinea.
facts.cite: Szűts T, Zhang J, Gallé-Szpisjak N, De Bakker D (2020) Jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) of the Papua New Guinean Mount Wilhelm and surrounding mountains. In: Robillard T, Legendre F, Villemant C, Leponce M (eds) Insects of Mount Wilhelm, Papua New Guinea, vol. 2. Mémoires du Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle 214: 521-555. Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris. ISBN 978-2-85653-836-4
facts.kp: Kausi, 5.73° S 145.33° E, 200 m a.s.l., 4th October 2013, Mixed lowland forest
facts.note: Holotype and one paratype from ~2800-3000 m (1968); two paratype males from 200 m lowland forest (2013). Described from males only; worth the owner's judgement whether the wide range is reliable.
facts.file: Szuts - 2020 - Jumping Spiders of Mount Wilhelm and Surrounding Mountains.txt

facts.t: Euryattus zilleae, described in 2020, lives in moss forest at about 2,800-3,000 m in the mountains of Papua New Guinea.
facts.cite: Szűts T, Zhang J, Gallé-Szpisjak N, De Bakker D (2020) Jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) of the Papua New Guinean Mount Wilhelm and surrounding mountains. In: Robillard T, Legendre F, Villemant C, Leponce M (eds) Insects of Mount Wilhelm, Papua New Guinea, vol. 2. Mémoires du Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle 214: 521-555. Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris. ISBN 978-2-85653-836-4
facts.where: p. 546, Euryattus zilleae, type material; etymology p. 548
facts.kp: mainly in moss forest, along the river, ~2800-3000 m a.s.l.
facts.note: Type series (5 males, 5 females besides holotype) collected in 1968. Named for the first author's daughter. Males have a shiny greenish metallic carapace.
facts.file: Szuts - 2020 - Jumping Spiders of Mount Wilhelm and Surrounding Mountains.txt

facts.t: Living Leptathamas males of New Guinea hold their legs in odd poses and walk jerkily, looking like little piles of debris.
facts.cite: Zhang J, Maddison WP (2012) New euophryine jumping spiders from Papua New Guinea (Araneae: Salticidae: Euophryinae). Zootaxa 3491: 1-74
facts.kp: males of Leptathamas resemble piles of debris, holding legs in strange poses
facts.note: Statement attributed to Maddison & Zhang 2011; repeated in Zhang & Maddison 2015 (Zootaxa 3938, p. 27, doi 10.11646/zootaxa.3938.1.1). Not an Australian genus.
facts.file: Zhang and Maddison - 2012 - New Euophryine Jumping Spiders from Papua New Guinea.txt

facts.t: Prószyński sank Canama into Bathippus in 1987; DNA later showed both are distinct genera, as Davies and Żabka had argued in 1989.
facts.cite: Zhang J, Maddison WP (2015) Genera of euophryine jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae), with a combined molecular-morphological phylogeny. Zootaxa 3938(1): 1-147
facts.kp: There has been a long debate on whether Bathippus and Canama should be merged
facts.note: Also fits Bathippus. Both genera are on the Australian list.
facts.file: Zhang - 2015 - Genera of euophryine jumping spiders (Araneae - Salticidae), with a combined molecular-morphological phylogeny.txt

facts.t: South-east Asian Parabathippus look much like Bathippus, but DNA places the two in different, not even closely related clades.
facts.cite: Zhang J, Maddison WP (2015) Genera of euophryine jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae), with a combined molecular-morphological phylogeny. Zootaxa 3938(1): 1-147
facts.kp: Parabathippus and Bathippus fall into different clades that are not even closely related
facts.note: Parabathippus was split from Bathippus by Zhang & Maddison 2012c (cited there); 'look much like' is my paraphrase of their 'superficially-similar' elongate body form with long male chelicerae (p. 13).
facts.file: Zhang - 2015 - Genera of euophryine jumping spiders (Araneae - Salticidae), with a combined molecular-morphological phylogeny.txt

facts.t: Zhang and Maddison argued in 2015 that Prostheclina, Maratus, Jotus and Barraina could all be merged into Saitis, but kept them apart.
facts.cite: Zhang J, Maddison WP (2015) Genera of euophryine jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae), with a combined molecular-morphological phylogeny. Zootaxa 3938(1): 1-147
facts.kp: A strong case can be made to merge all genera of this clade
facts.note: Also applies to Maratus, Jotus, Barraina, Saitis (and Hypoblemum, 'Lycidas', Maileus). Their reasons: near-identical genitalia and body form; courtship ornaments evolve fast. Related to existing Saitis-3 (Girard et al. 2021) but not a duplicate.
facts.file: Zhang - 2015 - Genera of euophryine jumping spiders (Araneae - Salticidae), with a combined molecular-morphological phylogeny.txt

facts.t: In 2012 Zhang and Maddison merged Zenodorus into Omoedus after DNA placed Omoedus inside Zenodorus; Prószyński (2017) kept them apart.
facts.cite: Zhang J, Maddison WP (2012) New euophryine jumping spiders from Papua New Guinea (Araneae: Salticidae: Euophryinae). Zootaxa 3491: 1-74
facts.kp: Omoedus and Pystira embedded within Zenodorus. Hence, we merge them as one genus
facts.note: Also fits Omoedus. Pystira was merged at the same time. Zhang & Maddison 2015 (p. 26) restate the merger; Prószyński 2017 (Ecologica Montenegrina 12, pp. 2, 5-7 and genus list) treats Omoedus (4 spp.) and Zenodorus (23 spp.) as separate. Both names are on the app's Australian list, so the fact is framed as history only; please check which placement the WSC currently follows before using.
facts.file: Zhang and Maddison - 2012 - New Euophryine Jumping Spiders from Papua New Guinea.txt

facts.t: In 2015 every Margaromma species except the type, M. funestum, was moved to Omoedus because their genitalia matched Omoedus.
facts.cite: Zhang J, Maddison WP (2015) Genera of euophryine jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae), with a combined molecular-morphological phylogeny. Zootaxa 3938(1): 1-147
facts.kp: other species currently in Margaromma have genitalia matching Omoedus
facts.note: Transferred: insultans, kochi, semirasus, sexualis, torquatus. Later authors may have moved species back or described new Margaromma; check the WSC before use.
facts.file: Zhang - 2015 - Genera of euophryine jumping spiders (Araneae - Salticidae), with a combined molecular-morphological phylogeny.txt

facts.t: Zhang and Maddison merged the genus Palpelius into Pristobaeus in 2015, following a suggestion from Jerzy Prószyński.
facts.cite: Zhang J, Maddison WP (2015) Genera of euophryine jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae), with a combined molecular-morphological phylogeny. Zootaxa 3938(1): 1-147
facts.kp: we follow Dr. Jerzy Prószyński's suggestion (pers. comm.) of merging these two genera
facts.note: Low appeal taxonomic note; notable only because the two authors usually disagree with Prószyński's genus concepts.
facts.file: Zhang - 2015 - Genera of euophryine jumping spiders (Araneae - Salticidae), with a combined molecular-morphological phylogeny.txt

facts.t: Phasmolia, described from Papua New Guinea in 2012, takes its name from Latin phasma, 'ghost', after its ghostly appearance.
facts.cite: Zhang J, Maddison WP (2012) New euophryine jumping spiders from Papua New Guinea (Araneae: Salticidae: Euophryinae). Zootaxa 3491: 1-74
facts.kp: derived from the Latin phasma (ghost), referring to the ghost-like appearance
facts.note: Type and only species described there: P. elegans ('elegant body form').
facts.file: Zhang and Maddison - 2012 - New Euophryine Jumping Spiders from Papua New Guinea.txt

facts.t: Viribestus, a New Guinea genus named in 2012, joins Latin virilis and bestia, 'virile animal', for the masculine nature of its male.
facts.cite: Zhang J, Maddison WP (2012) New euophryine jumping spiders from Papua New Guinea (Araneae: Salticidae: Euophryinae). Zootaxa 3491: 1-74
facts.kp: referring to the masculine nature of the male spider
facts.note: Described 2012 from a male collected at 2,300 m in Enga Province, PNG.
facts.file: Zhang and Maddison - 2012 - New Euophryine Jumping Spiders from Papua New Guinea.txt

facts.t: Zabkattus, a New Guinea leaf-litter genus named in 2012, joins Marek Żabka's name to '-attus', a common salticid genus ending.
facts.cite: Zhang J, Maddison WP (2012) New euophryine jumping spiders from Papua New Guinea (Araneae: Salticidae: Euophryinae). Zootaxa 3491: 1-74
facts.where: p. 66, Genus Zabkattus, Etymology and Diagnosis
facts.kp: combines "zabk" in honor of Dr. Marek Żabka
facts.note: Żabka is the main author of Australian salticid genera.
facts.file: Zhang and Maddison - 2012 - New Euophryine Jumping Spiders from Papua New Guinea.txt

facts.t: Chalcolemia was named in 2012 to echo the similar-looking Chalcolecta, though DNA shows the two are distinct genera.
facts.cite: Zhang J, Maddison WP (2012) New euophryine jumping spiders from Papua New Guinea (Araneae: Salticidae: Euophryinae). Zootaxa 3491: 1-74
facts.where: p. 20, Genus Chalcolemia, Etymology and Diagnosis
facts.kp: Chosen to resemble the name Chalcolecta
facts.note: Could also go on the Chalcolecta card (Australian list).
facts.file: Zhang and Maddison - 2012 - New Euophryine Jumping Spiders from Papua New Guinea.txt

facts.t: Males of typical Thorelliola carry 'horns' of enlarged setae on the clypeus, but some New Guinea species in the genus lack them.
facts.cite: Zhang J, Maddison WP (2015) Genera of euophryine jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae), with a combined molecular-morphological phylogeny. Zootaxa 3938(1): 1-147
facts.where: p. 33, Other genera from the Old World
facts.kp: Typical Thorelliola species usually have the male clypeus armed with "horns"
facts.note: Zhang & Maddison 2012 (p. 42) add that in some species the horns sit on a stalk (truncus).
facts.file: Zhang - 2015 - Genera of euophryine jumping spiders (Araneae - Salticidae), with a combined molecular-morphological phylogeny.txt

facts.t: In Athamas the front side eyes sit behind the front middle eyes in a row of their own, a layout that evolved more than once.
facts.cite: Zhang J, Maddison WP (2015) Genera of euophryine jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae), with a combined molecular-morphological phylogeny. Zootaxa 3938(1): 1-147
facts.kp: four-row eye arrangement has evolved more than once independently within the Euophryinae
facts.note: Shared with Bulolia and Leptathamas, and independently with Furculattus (a Diolenius relative). Not Australian genera.
facts.file: Zhang - 2015 - Genera of euophryine jumping spiders (Araneae - Salticidae), with a combined molecular-morphological phylogeny.txt

facts.t: Psenuc has a row of stridulatory spines on small bumps below its side eyes, which work against fine setae on the first femur.
facts.cite: Prószyński J (2017) Pragmatic classification of the World's Salticidae (Araneae). Ecologica Montenegrina 12: 1-133
facts.where: p. 5, Fig. 1A caption (E); p. 40, Fig. 18H caption; p. 42, group diagnosis
facts.kp: lateral subocular row of stridulatory spines (Fig. 18H) interacting with a row of microscopic microsetae
facts.note: Prószyński gives this as the character of his informal 'pseudiciines' group, illustrated with an Australian Psenuc sp. (photos R. Whyte). Related to existing Afraflacilla-1 (stridulatory organs in the Pseudicius group) but specific to Psenuc. Sound production itself is inferred from the structure, not recorded.
facts.file: Proszynski - 2017 - Pragmatic Classification of the Worlds Salticidae.txt

facts.t: The Asian jumping spider genus Hakka has colonised Hawaii and the Atlantic shores of North America.
facts.cite: Prószyński J (2017) Pragmatic classification of the World's Salticidae (Araneae). Ecologica Montenegrina 12: 1-133
facts.kp: Hakka occurs in China and is a colonist in Hawaii and Atlantic shores
facts.note: Hakka was described (Berry & Prószyński 2001) from Hawaii; type species H. himeshimensis (Bösenberg & Strand 1906). Not Australian.

facts.t: Junxattus, named in 2012 for arachnologist Junxia Zhang, was sunk into Laufeia in 2015 by Zhang herself, with Wayne Maddison.
facts.cite: Prószyński J (2018) Review of genera Evarcha and Nigorella, with comments on Emertonius, Padilothorax, Stagetillus, and description of five new genera and two new species (Araneae: Salticidae). Ecologica Montenegrina 16: 130-179
facts.kp: Genus Junxattus was named in honor of Dr Junxia Zhang
facts.note: The footnote says the dedication was left unexplained in the 2012 description because she objected. Synonymy: Zhang & Maddison 2015 (Zootaxa 3938, p. 30, doi 10.11646/zootaxa.3938.1.1); Prószyński 2018 rejects it. Laufeia is not on the Australian list.
facts.file: Proszynski - 2018 - Review of Evarcha and Nigorella and Related Genera.txt

facts.t: Nungia was described from Viet-Nam in 1985 and named after the Nung people who live there.
facts.cite: Żabka M (1985) Systematic and zoogeographic study on the family Salticidae (Araneae) from Viet-Nam. Annales Zoologici, Warszawa 39(11): 197-485
facts.kp: Named after the Nung nationality living in Viet-Nam.
facts.note: Described from a single female of N. epigynalis; Żabka notes a strongly flattened carapace and butterfly-shaped internal epigyne. Nungia is on the app's Australian list.

facts.t: Magyarus, a genus described from Viet-Nam in 1985, honours the Hungarian collectors Topál and Matskási.
facts.cite: Żabka M (1985) Systematic and zoogeographic study on the family Salticidae (Araneae) from Viet-Nam. Annales Zoologici, Warszawa 39(11): 197-485
facts.kp: Named in honour of Hungarians - TOPAL and MATSKASI, who collected
facts.note: Magyar = Hungarian. Monotypic; M. typicus was taken in pitfall traps. Not Australian. OCR of the footnote is rough ('ToPAL a11d MATSKASI'); key phrase normalised.

facts.t: Lechia, a 1985 genus from Viet-Nam now treated as a synonym of Laufeia, was named after Lech, the legendary founder of Poland.
facts.cite: Żabka M (1985) Systematic and zoogeographic study on the family Salticidae (Araneae) from Viet-Nam. Annales Zoologici, Warszawa 39(11): 197-485
facts.kp: Named after Lech, the legendary founder of Poland.
facts.note: Synonymy with Laufeia: per Prószyński 2018 (Ecologica Montenegrina 16, p. 177, item 7) the WSC follows Logunov in sinking Lechia into Laufeia; Prószyński rejects it. Check the WSC before use.

facts.t: Bianor's type species, B. maculatus, was first described from Australia by Eugen Keyserling in 1883, as Scythropa maculata.
facts.cite: Żabka M (1985) Systematic and zoogeographic study on the family Salticidae (Araneae) from Viet-Nam. Annales Zoologici, Warszawa 39(11): 197-485
facts.where: pp. 202-203, Bianor maculatus synonymy and remarks
facts.kp: B. maculatus is the type-species of the genus, known from Australia
facts.note: Synonymy line: '1883 Scythropa maculata KEYSERLING, Arachn. Austral.: 1447'. Żabka gives its range as Australia, New Caledonia and Samoa, and adds a single male from Viet-Nam (not used: may need re-checking). The Keyserling page itself is not in the owner's Koch/Keyserling scan (which covers pp. 1045-1158).
facts.file: Zabka - Systematic and Zoogeographic Study on the Family Salticidae.txt

facts.t: Żabka (1985) saw Synagelides, with dozens of closely related Himalayan species, as a young genus diversifying in high mountains.
facts.cite: Żabka M (1985) Systematic and zoogeographic study on the family Salticidae (Araneae) from Viet-Nam. Annales Zoologici, Warszawa 39(11): 197-485
facts.kp: some genera (Ptocasius, Synagelides) have several tens of closely related species
facts.note: Also applies to Ptocasius. Żabka's further claim that these genera have only single species beyond the Himalayas is out of date and was left out. Not Australian (Pseudosynagelides is a different genus).

facts.t: Describing Astia hariola in 1879, Ludwig Koch found it lives mostly under bark: a very quick spider, among the commonest and daintiest.
facts.cite: Koch L (1879) Die Arachniden Australiens, nach der Natur beschrieben und abgebildet, Lieferungen 24-25. Bauer & Raspe, Nürnberg, pp. 1045-1156
facts.where: p. 1155 (PDF p. 114), end of Astia hariola account
facts.kp: Astia hariola scheint sich meist unter Rinden aufzuhalten
facts.note: Original German: 'ein äusserst bewegliches, rasches Thierchen und wohl eine der gemeinsten, dabei aber auch der zierlichsten Arten'. Koch erected Astia (nov. genus) on p. 1152 with A. hariola as first species. The OCR of this passage is clean; the 1879 date is printed on the title of Lieferung 25 (from p. 1101).
facts.file: Die Arachniden Australiens - nach der Natur.txt

facts.t: Apricia jovialis was first described by Ludwig Koch in 1879, under the name Marptusa jovialis.
facts.cite: Koch L (1879) Die Arachniden Australiens, nach der Natur beschrieben und abgebildet, Lieferungen 24-25. Bauer & Raspe, Nürnberg, pp. 1045-1156
facts.where: p. 1109 (PDF p. 68), Marptusa jovialis n. spec.
facts.kp: Marptusa jovialis n. spec.
facts.note: Current name per existing facts Apricia-1/2 (Richardson 2016); I am relying on the epithet match and on Apricia jovialis being cited as (L. Koch, 1879). Complements Apricia-2 (later placements in Breda and Ocrisiona); Koch also lists one find under wood shavings.
